241	outbound <host>: <error> — the remote may have applied this call; the retry carries the same idempotency key
242	outbound <host>: timed out after <timeout> — the remote may have applied this call; the retry carries the same idempotency key
243	outbound <host>: the reply exceeded the <cap>-byte reply cap — the remote answered, so it applied this call; raise the cap with Host::max_reply_bytes (the retry carries the same idempotency key)
244	```
245	
246	The first line is a call whose connection never opened, so no byte of it was
247	sent: a refused connection, a failed DNS lookup or a failed TLS handshake. Its
248	`<error>` names which: `connection refused` in the sim, and in production
249	`could not connect: ` and the client's cause chain (`client error (Connect):
250	tcp connect error: Connection refused (os error 61)`, say), or `the outbound
251	runtime thread is gone` for a call the client's dead thread never took. The second is
252	every other transport failure's. `<timeout>` is the
253	job's `timeout` as Rust prints a `Duration` (`2s`, `1.5s`), and `<cap>` is the
254	host's reply cap in bytes.
255	
256	**Dead means no reply was settled.** It does not mean nothing happened at the
257	remote: a call whose reply was lost, or that timed out, may have been applied
258	there. The Dead job's `last_error` says which of the texts above ended it.
259	
260	**A remote that ignores the key is called again, and may bill again.** A retry
261	after a lost reply or a timeout sends the same request with the same key. A
262	remote with Stripe's semantics applies it once. Many remotes do not dedupe at
263	all, LLM APIs among them, so a lost reply there means a second completion is
264	requested and paid for. `settle` still commits at most once, so the app's state
265	stays exactly-once, but the remote's bill does not.
266	
267	**A crash-looping process calls again on every restart.** A crash is not an
268	attempt, as `JobError::Io` is not, so it spends nothing from `retry`. A job
269	whose dispatch keeps killing the process is called again each time it comes
270	back, without end.
271	
272	**Deploying a changed `call` under a key in flight.** A call in flight when the
273	process stops is called again by whichever binary comes up next. If that
274	binary's `call` builds different parameters, the remote receives the old key
275	with new parameters. Stripe-style APIs refuse that (the sim's `Idempotent`
276	model answers 409, §8), and `settle` receives the refusal as an ordinary reply.
277	Change what `call` sends the way "Changing a job's fields" below changes a
278	job's shape: drain the type's Pending jobs on the old binary first, or send the
279	new request from a new job type.
280	
281	**In a sim test.** A kernel over an app that mounts an outbound job needs an
282	`Outbound`, and every constructor refuses to build without one:
283	
284	<!-- pinned -->
285	```text
286	kernel: job <job> calls <host>, but this kernel has no Outbound — serve() supplies the production client; a sim test passes one: let outbound = sim.outbound(&app.outbound_hosts())?; Kernel::with_outbound(app, clock, Box::new(outbound))
287	```
288	
289	Register a model for each host with `sim.remote` (§8), then build the handle
290	from the app before the kernel takes it:
291	
292	```rust
293	use charpente::http::App;
294	use charpente::kernel::{Kernel, SimSource};
295	use charpente_sim::Sim;
296	
297	fn run_with_outbound(sim: &Sim, app: App, horizon_nanos: u64) -> std::io::Result<Kernel> {
298	    let outbound = sim.outbound(&app.outbound_hosts())?;
299	    let mut kernel = Kernel::with_outbound(app, Box::new(sim.clock()), Box::new(outbound))?;
300	    kernel.run(&mut SimSource::new(Box::new(sim.clock()), horizon_nanos))?;
301	    Ok(kernel)
302	}
303	```
304	
305	A node that also replicates or archives is built with `Kernel::builder(app,
306	clock)`, then any of `.replication(repl)`, `.archive(archive, store)` and
307	`.outbound(outbound)`, then `.build()`. `kernel.stats()` counts the arm's work
308	in `outbound_started` (calls started), `outbound_settled` (replies whose
309	`settle` committed), `outbound_failed` (every failure record: a failed or
310	refused `call`, a transport failure, a timeout, a failed `settle`),
311	`outbound_timed_out` and `outbound_late` (replies discarded, including any
312	still buffered when the node stopped being writable).
313	
314	### Changing a job's fields
315	
316	Every enqueue records the payload's shape — `Job::FINGERPRINT`, the structural
317	fingerprint `#[job]` computes from the fields (§12) — and a Pending job is only ever
318	decoded by a binary that compiled that same shape. A node about to become able to
319	dispatch refuses while any Pending job of a type it mounts was enqueued under another
320	shape. It checks at startup and at every moment its write gate opens (a witness gate
321	opening, a completed switchover), and `promote` checks before it changes anything:
322	
323	<!-- pinned -->
324	```text
325	<n> Pending "<job>" job(s) (ids <ids>) were enqueued under a different shape of <job> (recorded <recorded>; this binary <fingerprint>) — this binary will not decode them; run the binary that enqueued them until they are Done or Dead, then deploy this one, or restore whichever of <job>'s fields, its `global`/`scoped_by` declaration, its `outbound` declaration or its tenant type's `NAME` changed, and give the new shape its own #[job] type under a new name (GUIDE §6)
326	```
327	
328	A job's tenancy is part of its shape. A `scoped_by` job's fingerprint continues its
329	fields' fold over its tenant type's `NAME` (§16), so moving a job between `global` and
330	`scoped_by`, or to a tenant type with another `NAME`, is refused the same way. A deploy
331	therefore never hands a row enqueued with no tenant to a scoped `run`, one enqueued in a
332	tenant to a global one, or one enqueued in a tenant of one `NAME` to a job of another.
333	Respelling the `scoped_by` path is not a shape change while it names a type of the same
334	`NAME`: see below, after the scope-type refusal, for what that leaves unchecked.
335	
336	At most five ids are listed, then `…`. A job enqueued before shapes were recorded reads
337	`recorded none — enqueued before job shapes were tagged`, and it is refused the same way:
338	nothing decodes bytes it cannot prove are its own shape.
339	
340	- At startup, or when the write gate opens, the refusal stops the kernel, and a stopped
341	  kernel ends the process (§5).
342	- At `promote`, it answers `CtrlErr` prefixed `cannot promote:`, and the node stays a
343	  follower.
344	- A switchover is never refused partway. Once the old primary hands off it never resumes
345	  on its own (DESIGN §5 calls the hand-off its point of no return), so a refusal there
346	  would leave neither node writable. The switchover completes. The new primary's kernel
347	  then stops at the moment it becomes writable, with the refusal above, and its fix works
348	  from there: run the binary that enqueued the jobs on that node, now the primary, until
349	  they are Done or Dead. The old primary follows it throughout.
350	
351	Done and Dead rows are never decoded again and never refuse anything. A Pending row of a
352	job type this binary does not mount keeps the "not registered" path above.
353	
354	This binary never writes a foreign-shape row itself. `NAME` is the type's bare identifier,
355	so two `#[job]` types can share one: a route that still enqueues `v1::SendReceipt` in a
356	binary that mounts `v2::SendReceipt`, say. From `App::mount_jobs` on — whether or not a
357	kernel exists yet — an enqueue under another shape of a mounted name refuses its whole
358	transaction before anything is written:
359	
360	<!-- pinned -->
361	```text
362	job "<job>" was enqueued under a different shape of <job> than this binary mounts (enqueued <shape>; this binary <fingerprint>) — two #[job] types share the name <job>; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted type, or give the other type its own name (GUIDE §6)
363	```
364	
365	A route answers it with a 500 carrying that text, never the retryable storage-failure 500
366	(§5). Inside a job handler it is an attempt, like a panic: the job retries and then
367	dead-letters, with the text as its `last_error`. In a cron schedule's enqueue it stops the
368	kernel. An enqueue of a job type this binary does not mount at all is not refused here: it
369	commits and takes the "not registered" path.
370	
371	Tenancy has a twin of both refusals. `#[job]` fingerprints `scoped_by`, but a
372	hand-written `impl Job` can copy a mounted job's `NAME` and `FINGERPRINT` under the other
373	tenancy, and a hand-written `JobDef` can mount a job under the wrong one. Either would
374	hand the dispatcher a row with a tenant for a `global` job, or with none for a `scoped_by`
375	one. So an enqueue whose tenant presence disagrees with the mounted declaration refuses
376	its transaction the same way, and a Pending row that already disagrees is refused
377	wherever the shape refusal runs. `<presence>` is `a tenant` or `no tenant`, and
378	`<declaration>` is `` `global` `` or `` `scoped_by = Org` ``:
379	
380	<!-- pinned -->
381	```text
382	job "<job>" was enqueued with <presence>, but this binary mounts <job> as <declaration> under the same shape (<shape>) — a hand-written `impl Job` or `JobDef` contradicts <job>'s #[job]; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted type, give the other type its own name, or mount <job> as its #[job] declares it (GUIDE §6)
383	<n> Pending "<job>" job(s) (ids <ids>) carry <presence>, but this binary declares <job> <declaration> — the enqueue family writes a tenant exactly for a `scoped_by` job, so something that contradicts <job>'s #[job] wrote these rows: a hand-written `impl Job` or `JobDef`, or a raw store write; this binary will not dispatch them; mount <job> as its #[job] declares it, or restore the store from a replica or backup taken before these rows were written. For a follower, or a primary once a follower is promoted in its place, that is a re-seed: stop the node, delete its data dir, and restart it configured as a follower of the current primary so it snapshot-seeds from it, never with a primary config: the durable role file that outranks config is deleted with the data dir, so a cleared node started as a primary comes up as a second writable primary (GUIDE §6)
384	```
385	
386	Presence is not the whole of a tenant. A row records the tenant's id and not the scope type
387	it is an id of, and the dispatcher opens that id as the type the mounted job declares. The
388	fingerprint tells two scope types apart only by their `NAME`s. A `#[job(scoped_by = Desk)]`
389	in a module that says `use super::Board as Desk;` fingerprints with `Board`'s `NAME`, so it
390	is refused as another shape. But a `#[job]` whose `scoped_by` names another tenant type
391	with the same `NAME` fingerprints alike, and a hand-written `impl Job` can copy both
392	constants under any `type Scope`. Enqueued inside a tenant of that other type, either would
393	run the mounted job in the same id of the type it declares, a tenant nothing opened or
394	named for it. So an
395	enqueue whose job's scope type is not the one the mounted job declares refuses its
396	transaction the same way. `<scope>` is the enqueuing job's tenant type's `NAME` and `<declared>` the
397	mounted one's (§16); `<id>` is the tenant id. The two NAMEs can be equal. A hand-built `JobDef` that
398	names one type and carries another's `scope_type` is refused here on the honest enqueue, which is why
399	the text says "with another scope type" and lists that cause:
400	
401	<!-- pinned -->
402	```text
403	job "<job>" was enqueued in a `<scope>` tenant, but this binary mounts <job> as `scoped_by = <declared>` with another scope type under the same shape (<shape>) — a job row records its tenant's id and not its type, so tenant <id> would be read as the mounted declaration's type, not the one it was enqueued in; either a type standing in for <job>'s #[job] was enqueued (a hand-written `impl Job`, or a #[job] whose `scoped_by` names another tenant type with the same `NAME`), or a hand-written `JobDef` mounts <job> under a `scope_type` its #[job] does not declare; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted <job> from a `<declared>` scope, give the other type its own name, or mount <job> as its #[job] declares it (GUIDE §6)
404	```
405	
406	One door is left inside a binary, and it is a hand-built `JobDef`. Its fields are public,
407	so `JobDef { glue: <another job's glue>, ..<File as JobEntry>::def() }` mounts a glue that
408	opens a different scope type than `scope_type` names, and so does a `JobDef` whose
409	`scoped_by` and `scope_type` both name a type its glue does not open. `Group::stage` holds
410	the enqueuer to `scope_type`, and a scoped job's glue opens its row's tenant through
411	`JobScope::open`, which asserts that the type it opens is `scope_type`. The assert runs
412	inside the attempt, so the job retries and then dead-letters, and nothing runs in either
413	tenant. Its `last_error`, for `File`'s `JobDef` carrying a `Board` job's glue, is below.
414	`<path>` is `Board`'s `std::any::type_name`, printed beside its `NAME` so that a glue whose
415	type shares the declared `NAME` still reads as two types:
416	
417	<!-- pinned -->
418	```text
419	handler panicked: contract: the glue mounted for job "File" opened its tenant 31 as `Board` (the tenant type `<path>`), but that `JobDef` declares `scoped_by = Desk` with a `scope_type` that is not `<path>` — a hand-built `JobDef` whose `glue` or `scope_type` disagrees with its #[job] (a glue taken from another job, or another type's `TypeId`); this attempt wrote nothing, and every retry fails the same way — mount File through `jobs![…]`, which builds its `JobDef` from its #[job] (GUIDE §6)
420	```
421	
422	A `JobDef` whose glue and `scope_type` name the same other type passes the assert. Nothing
423	can tell it apart, and it does not cross a tenant: `Group::stage` held the enqueuer to
424	that same type, so the job runs in the tenant it was enqueued in, only with another job's
425	code. `jobs![…]` builds every `JobDef` from its `#[job]`, and it is the way to mount one.
426	
427	This one has no startup twin, because a row carries no type to compare, only the `NAME`
428	its fingerprint mixes. The check runs where both types are known, at the enqueue, in a
429	binary that mounts the job. At startup the dispatching binary compares a Pending row's
430	shape, so a row whose job named a tenant type of another `NAME` is refused there by the
431	foreign-shape refusal above. That covers the refactor that turns a job module's `use
432	billing::Org;` into `use crm::Org;`, whenever the two types' NAMEs differ. What a later
433	binary that mounts the name dispatches unchecked, in the scope type it declares, is a row
434	whose shape matches:
435	
436	- a row a hand-written `impl Job` enqueued from a binary that did not mount the job name,
437	  copying the job's `NAME` and `FINGERPRINT` under another `type Scope`;
438	- a row enqueued under a tenant type with the same `NAME` as the mounted one. A `NAME` is
439	  the tenant's identity, so this is the same tenant by declaration: giving a type another
440	  type's `NAME` declares it that tenant, and one app cannot mount both (§16).
441	
442	Where the recorded shape matches the mounted one, neither is refused, at startup or at
443	dispatch. So before a deploy that mounts a scoped job the running binary does not mount,
444	drain that job: run the binary that enqueued its Pending rows until every one is Done or
445	Dead, the first way through a shape change below.
446	
447	There are two ways through a shape change:
448	
449	- **Drain first.** Run the binary that enqueued them — the old one after an upgrade, the
450	  newer one after a rollback — until every Pending job of the type is Done or Dead (each
451	  reaches one within its retry policy), then deploy. In a replicated pair, drain on the
452	  primary before a switchover onto a follower running another shape, or that follower
453	  stops as described above.
454	- **A new type.** Leave the old type's fields alone, put the new fields in a new `#[job]`
455	  type under a new name, mount both, and switch enqueues to the new one. The name is not
456	  optional: `NAME` is the type's own identifier, and `mount_jobs` panics on two jobs of
457	  one name. The old type keeps dispatching its rows, because their shape is still its
458	  own; remove it once none are Pending.
459	
460	What the fingerprint cannot see, a change inside a type a field holds, is in §12.
461	
462	### What `#[job]` rejects
463	
464	Every rejection is a compile error naming the contract and the fix. The first is the
465	one every job meets once, and the next three are its neighbours:
466	
467	<!-- pinned -->
468	```text
469	`<job>` declares no tenancy — a job says which. Add one of these to its `#[job(…)]`, keeping any arguments it already has: `scoped_by = Org` if it acts inside one tenant (it is enqueued from inside that tenant's scope, and its `run` receives that tenant's `ScopedTx`), or `global` if it belongs to no tenant (the only kind cron can schedule). Neither is the default.
470	`global` and `scoped_by = <scope>` on one job — a job is one or the other; drop one
471	`global` given twice — write it once
472	`scoped_by` given twice — write it once
473	```
474	
475	The second every job meets once too, right after the first: a job that names its
476	tenancy and not what its Dead means ("What a job's Dead means" above). Its
477	neighbours refuse both stances at once and either one twice:
478	
479	<!-- pinned -->
480	```text
481	`<job>` declares no Dead stance — a job says what its Dead means. Add one of these to its `#[job(…)]`, keeping any arguments it already has: `on_dead` if the app must act when the job's retries run out (the job then has `fn on_dead(self, tx: &mut Tx, dead: Dead<Self>) -> Result<(), JobError>`, whose writes commit with the Dead mark), or `retain_dead` if the Dead row, kept with its last error, is all that should happen. Neither is the default.
482	`on_dead` and `retain_dead` are two answers to one question — keep the one this job means
483	`on_dead` given twice — write it once
484	`retain_dead` given twice — write it once
485	```
486	
487	A `scoped_by` job enqueued where no tenant is named — `tx.enqueue` on a bare `Tx`, or
488	`App::schedule` — is an unsatisfied bound, and rustc prints this note with your job and
489	scope in place of `<job>` and `<scope>` (§16 shows it rendered):
490	
491	<!-- pinned -->
492	```text
493	`<job>` is a tenant-scoped job (`#[job(scoped_by = <scope>)]`) and a bare `Tx` names no tenant to run it in
494	enqueue it from inside the tenant it acts in, and it runs in that tenant:
495	    let mut tx = tx.scope::<<scope>>(scope, ctx)?;
496	    tx.enqueue(job);
497	or fan it out from a `cross_tenant` route or job, naming the tenant:
498	    tx.enqueue_in::<<scope>>(scope, job, cap);
499	cron (`App::schedule`) enqueues on a bare `Tx`, so it schedules `global` jobs only
500	```
501	
502	The rest are about the attribute's syntax and the struct's shape:
503	
504	```rust,ignore
505	// a word the attribute does not recognise
506	#[job(bogus)]
507	struct Foo {}
508	// "a job declares `global` or `scoped_by = <Type>` and one of `on_dead` /
509	//  `retain_dead`, and may add `cross_tenant`, `retry(max = <int>, backoff =
510	//  \"<n><unit>\")` (unit is one of ms, s, m, h), and `outbound = \"<host>\"`
511	//  with an optional `timeout = \"<n><unit>\"`, in any order — e.g.
512	//  `#[job(scoped_by = Org, retain_dead, retry(max = 3, backoff = \"10s\"))]`,
513	//  `#[job(global, cross_tenant, on_dead)]` or `#[job(scoped_by = Org, on_dead,
514	//  outbound = \"api.stripe.com\", timeout = \"30s\")]`"
515	
516	// backoff with no unit suffix
517	#[job(global, retain_dead, retry(max = 3, backoff = "10"))]
518	struct Bar {}
519	// "backoff \"10\" has no unit — a job declares `global` or `scoped_by =
520	//  <Type>` and one of `on_dead` / `retain_dead`, and may add `cross_tenant`,
521	//  `retry(max = <int>, backoff = \"<n><unit>\")` (unit is one of ms, s, m, h),
522	//  and `outbound = \"<host>\"` with an optional `timeout = \"<n><unit>\"`, in
523	//  any order — e.g. `#[job(scoped_by = Org, retain_dead, retry(max = 3,
524	//  backoff = \"10s\"))]`, `#[job(global, cross_tenant, on_dead)]` or
525	//  `#[job(scoped_by = Org, on_dead, outbound = \"api.stripe.com\", timeout =
526	//  \"30s\")]`"
527	
528	// enums and unions cannot be job payloads
529	#[job(global, retain_dead)]
530	enum Baz {
531	    A,
532	}
533	// "#[job] applies to structs — enums and unions cannot be job payloads"
534	```
535	
536	## 7. Cron
537	
538	Cron rides the same kernel loop as HTTP requests and jobs (§5, §6) — a
539	schedule is a row, and a due tick is one transaction that advances the
540	schedule and enqueues a job through the exact same path `tx.enqueue` uses:
541	a recurring enqueuer, inheriting retry and observability for free.

`enqueue`, `enqueue_keyed`, `enqueue_in` and cron take outbound jobs unchanged.

```rust
use charpente::kernel::JobError;
use charpente::outbound::{Call, IdempotencyKey, Reply};
use charpente::{Tx, job};

#[job(
    global,
    retain_dead,
    outbound = "pay.test",
    retry(max = 3, backoff = "1s"),
    timeout = "2s"
)]
struct Charge {
    cents: u64,
}

impl Charge {
    fn call(&self, _tx: &Tx, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError> {
        Ok(Some(
            Call::post("/charges")
                .header("idempotency-key", key.as_str())
                .form(&[("amount", self.cents.to_string())]),
        ))
    }

    fn settle(self, _tx: &mut Tx, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError> {
        match reply.status() {
            200 => Ok(()),
            s => Err(JobError::app(format!("pay.test answered {s}"))),
        }
    }
}

#[job(global, retain_dead, outbound = "mail.test")]
struct Mail {}

impl Mail {
    fn call(&self, _tx: &Tx, _key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError> {
        Ok(None)
    }

    fn settle(self, _tx: &mut Tx, _reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError> {
        Ok(())
    }
}

// One `Host` per host a mounted job calls, in any order.
use charpente::core::db::Schema;
use charpente::core::io::{Disk, Entropy};
use charpente::http::{App, AppConfig};
use charpente::jobs;
use charpente::outbound::Host;

fn build_app(disk: Box<dyn Disk>, entropy: Box<dyn Entropy>) -> std::io::Result<App> {
    Ok(App::open(disk, Schema::new(), entropy, AppConfig::default())?
        .mount_jobs(jobs![Charge, Mail])
        .outbound(Host::new("pay.test").bearer_env("PAY_KEY").max_reply_bytes(1 << 20))
        .outbound(Host::new("mail.test").header_env("X-Postmark-Server-Token", "POSTMARK_TOKEN"))
        .outbound_max_in_flight(64))
}
```

The two methods have exactly these shapes. A `global` job's:

```text
fn call(&self, tx: &Tx, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError>
fn settle(self, tx: &mut Tx, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError>
```

A `scoped_by = Org` job's take its tenant's `ScopedTx`, as its `run` would:

```text
fn call(&self, tx: &ScopedTx<'_, '_, Org>, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError>
fn settle(self, tx: &mut ScopedTx<'_, '_, Org>, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError>
```

`call` takes a shared `&Tx`, so it reads and cannot write: a `tx.put` inside it is
a compile error, and so is a scoped job's `call` or `settle` taking a bare `Tx`
(§9 lists both). Whatever the call's outcome should change, `settle` writes. When
there is nothing to call any more (the order was cancelled after the enqueue, say),
`call` returns `Ok(None)`, and the job is done without a call.

`key` is the job's idempotency key. The platform mints it when the job is
enqueued, 16 bytes from the node's entropy rendered as 32 lowercase hex
characters, and it stays the same across every retry and every re-dispatch after
a crash or a failover. charpente sends it nowhere by itself: `call` places it
where the remote reads one, the `idempotency-key` header above or a field of the
body, so a remote that honours it applies a repeated request once. It is not
`enqueue_keyed`'s app key.

The minted key belongs to one job and covers that job's retries and
re-dispatches. A redrive from the job's own `on_dead` hook, `tx.reissue_at` or
`tx.reissue_after` ("Re-issuing a dead job" above), resends the same request under
the same key: it copies the dead job's name, payload bytes and key, and never draws
one, so a remote that honours keys applies the effect once even if a failover
leaves one timeline re-dispatching the original while another calls the re-issue.
Any other re-issue, an effect the app enqueues again from a route, a cron tick or
another job, is a new job with a new key. So its `call` must send an id of the
effect itself, a field of the payload, or a remote that honours keys applies the
effect twice.

Because the key is drawn as the enqueue is staged, an outbound job is enqueued
only in a transaction the platform opens: a route's, a job's or a cron tick's.
`Db::transact` and `Db::begin_group` (§4) cannot mint, and a fresh outbound enqueue
inside either panics with a contract message (§9); a re-issue's key is copied from
its Dead record, not drawn, so it stages there. Code that opens its own group
stages through `Db::begin_group_minting` instead, and a test seeds an outbound job
through `App::transact_for_tests`, which the message names.

The request is built on the declared host, which is never runtime data:
`Call::get`, `post`, `put`, `patch` and `delete` take a path that begins with `/`.
`.header(name, value)` sends the name lowercase. `.json(&value)` and
`.form(&[(name, value)])` set the body and its `content-type`, and `.body(bytes)`
sets a raw body with none. A call carries one `content-type`, so setting another
(through `json`, `form` or `header`) replaces the earlier one. `settle` receives
the reply of any status, a 3xx included, since a redirect is never followed:
`reply.status()`, `reply.header(name)` (the first of that name, case-insensitively),
`reply.body()`, and `reply.json::<T>()`, which is a `JobError::App` when the body is
not `T`'s JSON.

The host is a bare DNS name like `api.stripe.com`. A scheme, port, path or
userinfo in it is a compile error, because where the host resolves is the
operator's to say. `timeout` bounds the wait for the remote's reply, with
`backoff`'s syntax; it defaults to 30 s, and it is refused on a job without
`outbound`. `cross_tenant` beside `outbound` is refused: an outbound call runs in
the one tenant its job was enqueued in. An outbound job's `impl` that has `run`
instead of `call` and `settle` fails to compile too. §9 lists each refusal's
text.

Outbound-ness is part of a job's shape: an outbound job's `FINGERPRINT` continues
its fingerprint as a pure job (`charpente::core::db::outbound_fingerprint`), so
adding `outbound` to a job, or removing it, is a shape change. It is refused while
Pending jobs of the old shape exist, and the ways through are the two "Changing a
job's fields" below describes: drain first, or a new type. The host is not part of
the shape, so changing the host is not refused.

`#[job]` writes a job's `OUTBOUND` constant and its mounted `JobDef.outbound` from
the one declaration, so the two agree. A hand-written `impl Job` or a hand-built
`JobDef` can make them disagree under the same shape, and dispatch routes a row by
whether its enqueue minted a key, so that row would reach a glue the mounted job does
not have. From `App::mount_jobs` on, such an enqueue refuses its whole transaction
before any key is drawn, and is answered the way the shape refusal in "Changing a
job's fields" below is. `<value>` is `true` or `false`, and `<declaration>` is
`a pure job` or `` `outbound = "<host>"` ``:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
job "<job>" was enqueued with `OUTBOUND = <value>`, but this binary mounts <job> as <declaration> under the same shape (<shape>) — dispatch routes a row by whether its enqueue minted an idempotency key, which only an `OUTBOUND = true` enqueue does, so this row would reach a glue the mounted <job> does not have; a hand-written `impl Job` or `JobDef` contradicts <job>'s #[job]; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted type, give the other type its own name, or mount <job> as its #[job] declares it (GUIDE §6)
```

A row that already disagrees, enqueued by a binary that did not mount the name,
stops the kernel at dispatch with a `contract:` panic that names the job and the
fix, rather than spending its retries on a glue that cannot run.

### Declaring the hosts

An outbound job names its host; the `App` says how to reach it. Declare one
`Host` per host that a mounted job calls, as `build_app` at the end of the `Charge`
block above does.

The builders are `bearer_env(var)`, `header_env(name, var)`, `basic_env(user_var,
pass_var)`, `max_request_bytes(n)` and `max_reply_bytes(n)`. A credential is the
NAME of an environment variable. `serve` reads each value once, when it starts
(as `serve_with`, `serve_replicated`, `backup` and `archive` do, §5), and the
value never enters the log, the sim, an error text or `describe`, which lists
variable and header names only. A variable that is unset, empty, holds a
control character or is not UTF-8 refuses the start before the listener is
bound (a `basic_env` pair included, though base64 would carry a control
character: one there is a pasted newline, not a credential). The one
exception is a `basic_env` password, which may be empty, since APIs that take
the key as the username (Stripe's `-u sk_…:`) send `user:`:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
outbound: <var> is unset — host <host> needs it for job <job>
outbound: <var> is set but empty — host <host> needs it for job <job>
outbound: <var> holds a control character (a trailing newline, say) or is not UTF-8 — host <host> needs it for job <job>; set it to the credential alone
```

`<job>` is the first mounted job that calls `<host>`. The caps default to
1 MiB and 4 MiB, and neither passes `MAX_CAP_BYTES` (8 MiB).

Each host is reached at `https://<host>:443` over HTTP/1.1, its certificate
verified against Mozilla's root store (`webpki-roots`, so the answer does not
vary with the machine's OS). An operator moves the address with
`--outbound-base` and adds a CA with `--outbound-ca` (§5); neither changes the
name that TLS verifies. No redirect is followed, so a 3xx is a reply that
`settle` reads. The client neither retries nor times out on its own: both are
the kernel's, through `retry` and `timeout`.

The two sets must match both ways, checked when the kernel is built, so mount
order is free. A called host with no entry is refused with
`kernel: job <job> calls <host>, which has no Host entry — add
app.outbound(Host::new("<host>")) with the credentials it needs (GUIDE §6)`,
and an entry no mounted job calls with `kernel:
app.outbound(Host::new("<host>")) declares a host no mounted job calls —
remove it, or mount the job that calls it`. Declaring one host twice panics
at `app.outbound`. `app.outbound_hosts()` returns the hosts the mounted jobs
call, sorted: the list `sim.outbound` takes.

`app.outbound_max_in_flight(n)` sets how many calls a node keeps in flight at
once (default 64, `charpente::outbound::DEFAULT_MAX_IN_FLIGHT`). A due
outbound job waits while the table is full, and a pure job never waits behind
it.

### When a call fails

The kernel starts a call only after the transaction that ran `call` has
committed, so a call never goes out on state that did not become durable,
including a write by another job in the same batch that `call` read. It waits
for the reply outside any transaction, for at most `timeout`, and hands the
reply to `settle`. An attempt below counts against `retry` the way a failed
`run` does: `attempts` increments, `last_error` names the failure, and the job
waits out its backoff or goes Dead, running its `on_dead` hook if it declares one
("What a job's Dead means" above). Every retry carries the job's key unchanged.

| What happens | An attempt? | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `call` returns `Ok(None)` | — | Done; no call |
| `call` returns `Err(JobError::App)` or panics (`call panicked: …`) | yes | failure record; no call |
| `call` builds a request its `Host` entry refuses | yes | failure record naming the rule; no call |
| `call` returns `Err(JobError::Io)` | no | bubbles: restart-and-recover |
| a transport failure: refused, TLS, DNS, a reset, a reply over the cap | yes | failure record |
| `timeout` passes with no reply | yes | the call is cancelled; failure record |
| a reply for a call that already timed out or was dropped | — | discarded, counted in `outbound_late` |
| `settle` returns `Ok` | — | its writes and the Done mark commit as one record |
| `settle` returns `Err(JobError::App)` or panics (`settle panicked: …`) | yes | its writes discarded; failure record |
| `settle` returns `Err(JobError::Io)` | no | bubbles; still Pending, called again after the restart |
| the process crashes with calls in flight | no | the Pending jobs are called again on restart |
| the node stops being writable (a switchover, a demotion) | no | its calls in flight are dropped; the next writable node calls again |
| the node is restored from its archive | no | Pending rows keep their key, so a re-call is the same request |

An attempt that may have reached the remote says so. Only a refused connection
certainly did not, so it is the one text that says the call never arrived:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
outbound <host>: <error> — the call did not reach the remote
outbound <host>: <error> — the remote may have applied this call; the retry carries the same idempotency key
outbound <host>: timed out after <timeout> — the remote may have applied this call; the retry carries the same idempotency key
outbound <host>: the reply exceeded the <cap>-byte reply cap — the remote answered, so it applied this call; raise the cap with Host::max_reply_bytes (the retry carries the same idempotency key)
```

The first line is a call whose connection never opened, so no byte of it was
sent: a refused connection, a failed DNS lookup or a failed TLS handshake. Its
`<error>` names which: `connection refused` in the sim, and in production
`could not connect: ` and the client's cause chain (`client error (Connect):
tcp connect error: Connection refused (os error 61)`, say), or `the outbound
runtime thread is gone` for a call the client's dead thread never took. The second is
every other transport failure's. `<timeout>` is the
job's `timeout` as Rust prints a `Duration` (`2s`, `1.5s`), and `<cap>` is the
host's reply cap in bytes.

**Dead means no reply was settled.** It does not mean nothing happened at the
remote: a call whose reply was lost, or that timed out, may have been applied
there. The Dead job's `last_error` says which of the texts above ended it.

**A remote that ignores the key is called again, and may bill again.** A retry
after a lost reply or a timeout sends the same request with the same key. A
remote with Stripe's semantics applies it once. Many remotes do not dedupe at
all, LLM APIs among them, so a lost reply there means a second completion is
requested and paid for. `settle` still commits at most once, so the app's state
stays exactly-once, but the remote's bill does not.

**A crash-looping process calls again on every restart.** A crash is not an
attempt, as `JobError::Io` is not, so it spends nothing from `retry`. A job
whose dispatch keeps killing the process is called again each time it comes
back, without end.

**Deploying a changed `call` under a key in flight.** A call in flight when the
process stops is called again by whichever binary comes up next. If that
binary's `call` builds different parameters, the remote receives the old key
with new parameters. Stripe-style APIs refuse that (the sim's `Idempotent`
model answers 409, §8), and `settle` receives the refusal as an ordinary reply.
Change what `call` sends the way "Changing a job's fields" below changes a
job's shape: drain the type's Pending jobs on the old binary first, or send the
new request from a new job type.

**In a sim test.** A kernel over an app that mounts an outbound job needs an
`Outbound`, and every constructor refuses to build without one:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
kernel: job <job> calls <host>, but this kernel has no Outbound — serve() supplies the production client; a sim test passes one: let outbound = sim.outbound(&app.outbound_hosts())?; Kernel::with_outbound(app, clock, Box::new(outbound))
```

Register a model for each host with `sim.remote` (§8), then build the handle
from the app before the kernel takes it:

```rust
use charpente::http::App;
use charpente::kernel::{Kernel, SimSource};
use charpente_sim::Sim;

fn run_with_outbound(sim: &Sim, app: App, horizon_nanos: u64) -> std::io::Result<Kernel> {
    let outbound = sim.outbound(&app.outbound_hosts())?;
    let mut kernel = Kernel::with_outbound(app, Box::new(sim.clock()), Box::new(outbound))?;
    kernel.run(&mut SimSource::new(Box::new(sim.clock()), horizon_nanos))?;
    Ok(kernel)
}
```

A node that also replicates or archives is built with `Kernel::builder(app,
clock)`, then any of `.replication(repl)`, `.archive(archive, store)` and
`.outbound(outbound)`, then `.build()`. `kernel.stats()` counts the arm's work
in `outbound_started` (calls started), `outbound_settled` (replies whose
`settle` committed), `outbound_failed` (every failure record: a failed or
refused `call`, a transport failure, a timeout, a failed `settle`),
`outbound_timed_out` and `outbound_late` (replies discarded, including any
still buffered when the node stopped being writable).

### Changing a job's fields

Every enqueue records the payload's shape — `Job::FINGERPRINT`, the structural
fingerprint `#[job]` computes from the fields (§12) — and a Pending job is only ever
decoded by a binary that compiled that same shape. A node about to become able to
dispatch refuses while any Pending job of a type it mounts was enqueued under another
shape. It checks at startup and at every moment its write gate opens (a witness gate
opening, a completed switchover), and `promote` checks before it changes anything:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
<n> Pending "<job>" job(s) (ids <ids>) were enqueued under a different shape of <job> (recorded <recorded>; this binary <fingerprint>) — this binary will not decode them; run the binary that enqueued them until they are Done or Dead, then deploy this one, or restore whichever of <job>'s fields, its `global`/`scoped_by` declaration, its `outbound` declaration or its tenant type's `NAME` changed, and give the new shape its own #[job] type under a new name (GUIDE §6)
```

A job's tenancy is part of its shape. A `scoped_by` job's fingerprint continues its
fields' fold over its tenant type's `NAME` (§16), so moving a job between `global` and
`scoped_by`, or to a tenant type with another `NAME`, is refused the same way. A deploy
therefore never hands a row enqueued with no tenant to a scoped `run`, one enqueued in a
tenant to a global one, or one enqueued in a tenant of one `NAME` to a job of another.
Respelling the `scoped_by` path is not a shape change while it names a type of the same
`NAME`: see below, after the scope-type refusal, for what that leaves unchecked.

At most five ids are listed, then `…`. A job enqueued before shapes were recorded reads
`recorded none — enqueued before job shapes were tagged`, and it is refused the same way:
nothing decodes bytes it cannot prove are its own shape.

- At startup, or when the write gate opens, the refusal stops the kernel, and a stopped
  kernel ends the process (§5).
- At `promote`, it answers `CtrlErr` prefixed `cannot promote:`, and the node stays a
  follower.
- A switchover is never refused partway. Once the old primary hands off it never resumes
  on its own (DESIGN §5 calls the hand-off its point of no return), so a refusal there
  would leave neither node writable. The switchover completes. The new primary's kernel
  then stops at the moment it becomes writable, with the refusal above, and its fix works
  from there: run the binary that enqueued the jobs on that node, now the primary, until
  they are Done or Dead. The old primary follows it throughout.

Done and Dead rows are never decoded again and never refuse anything. A Pending row of a
job type this binary does not mount keeps the "not registered" path above.

This binary never writes a foreign-shape row itself. `NAME` is the type's bare identifier,
so two `#[job]` types can share one: a route that still enqueues `v1::SendReceipt` in a
binary that mounts `v2::SendReceipt`, say. From `App::mount_jobs` on — whether or not a
kernel exists yet — an enqueue under another shape of a mounted name refuses its whole
transaction before anything is written:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
job "<job>" was enqueued under a different shape of <job> than this binary mounts (enqueued <shape>; this binary <fingerprint>) — two #[job] types share the name <job>; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted type, or give the other type its own name (GUIDE §6)
```

A route answers it with a 500 carrying that text, never the retryable storage-failure 500
(§5). Inside a job handler it is an attempt, like a panic: the job retries and then
dead-letters, with the text as its `last_error`. In a cron schedule's enqueue it stops the
kernel. An enqueue of a job type this binary does not mount at all is not refused here: it
commits and takes the "not registered" path.

Tenancy has a twin of both refusals. `#[job]` fingerprints `scoped_by`, but a
hand-written `impl Job` can copy a mounted job's `NAME` and `FINGERPRINT` under the other
tenancy, and a hand-written `JobDef` can mount a job under the wrong one. Either would
hand the dispatcher a row with a tenant for a `global` job, or with none for a `scoped_by`
one. So an enqueue whose tenant presence disagrees with the mounted declaration refuses
its transaction the same way, and a Pending row that already disagrees is refused
wherever the shape refusal runs. `<presence>` is `a tenant` or `no tenant`, and
`<declaration>` is `` `global` `` or `` `scoped_by = Org` ``:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
job "<job>" was enqueued with <presence>, but this binary mounts <job> as <declaration> under the same shape (<shape>) — a hand-written `impl Job` or `JobDef` contradicts <job>'s #[job]; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted type, give the other type its own name, or mount <job> as its #[job] declares it (GUIDE §6)
<n> Pending "<job>" job(s) (ids <ids>) carry <presence>, but this binary declares <job> <declaration> — the enqueue family writes a tenant exactly for a `scoped_by` job, so something that contradicts <job>'s #[job] wrote these rows: a hand-written `impl Job` or `JobDef`, or a raw store write; this binary will not dispatch them; mount <job> as its #[job] declares it, or restore the store from a replica or backup taken before these rows were written. For a follower, or a primary once a follower is promoted in its place, that is a re-seed: stop the node, delete its data dir, and restart it configured as a follower of the current primary so it snapshot-seeds from it, never with a primary config: the durable role file that outranks config is deleted with the data dir, so a cleared node started as a primary comes up as a second writable primary (GUIDE §6)
```

Presence is not the whole of a tenant. A row records the tenant's id and not the scope type
it is an id of, and the dispatcher opens that id as the type the mounted job declares. The
fingerprint tells two scope types apart only by their `NAME`s. A `#[job(scoped_by = Desk)]`
in a module that says `use super::Board as Desk;` fingerprints with `Board`'s `NAME`, so it
is refused as another shape. But a `#[job]` whose `scoped_by` names another tenant type
with the same `NAME` fingerprints alike, and a hand-written `impl Job` can copy both
constants under any `type Scope`. Enqueued inside a tenant of that other type, either would
run the mounted job in the same id of the type it declares, a tenant nothing opened or
named for it. So an
enqueue whose job's scope type is not the one the mounted job declares refuses its
transaction the same way. `<scope>` is the enqueuing job's tenant type's `NAME` and `<declared>` the
mounted one's (§16); `<id>` is the tenant id. The two NAMEs can be equal. A hand-built `JobDef` that
names one type and carries another's `scope_type` is refused here on the honest enqueue, which is why
the text says "with another scope type" and lists that cause:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
job "<job>" was enqueued in a `<scope>` tenant, but this binary mounts <job> as `scoped_by = <declared>` with another scope type under the same shape (<shape>) — a job row records its tenant's id and not its type, so tenant <id> would be read as the mounted declaration's type, not the one it was enqueued in; either a type standing in for <job>'s #[job] was enqueued (a hand-written `impl Job`, or a #[job] whose `scoped_by` names another tenant type with the same `NAME`), or a hand-written `JobDef` mounts <job> under a `scope_type` its #[job] does not declare; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted <job> from a `<declared>` scope, give the other type its own name, or mount <job> as its #[job] declares it (GUIDE §6)
```

One door is left inside a binary, and it is a hand-built `JobDef`. Its fields are public,
so `JobDef { glue: <another job's glue>, ..<File as JobEntry>::def() }` mounts a glue that
opens a different scope type than `scope_type` names, and so does a `JobDef` whose
`scoped_by` and `scope_type` both name a type its glue does not open. `Group::stage` holds
the enqueuer to `scope_type`, and a scoped job's glue opens its row's tenant through
`JobScope::open`, which asserts that the type it opens is `scope_type`. The assert runs
inside the attempt, so the job retries and then dead-letters, and nothing runs in either
tenant. Its `last_error`, for `File`'s `JobDef` carrying a `Board` job's glue, is below.
`<path>` is `Board`'s `std::any::type_name`, printed beside its `NAME` so that a glue whose
type shares the declared `NAME` still reads as two types:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
handler panicked: contract: the glue mounted for job "File" opened its tenant 31 as `Board` (the tenant type `<path>`), but that `JobDef` declares `scoped_by = Desk` with a `scope_type` that is not `<path>` — a hand-built `JobDef` whose `glue` or `scope_type` disagrees with its #[job] (a glue taken from another job, or another type's `TypeId`); this attempt wrote nothing, and every retry fails the same way — mount File through `jobs![…]`, which builds its `JobDef` from its #[job] (GUIDE §6)
```

A `JobDef` whose glue and `scope_type` name the same other type passes the assert. Nothing
can tell it apart, and it does not cross a tenant: `Group::stage` held the enqueuer to
that same type, so the job runs in the tenant it was enqueued in, only with another job's
code. `jobs![…]` builds every `JobDef` from its `#[job]`, and it is the way to mount one.

This one has no startup twin, because a row carries no type to compare, only the `NAME`
its fingerprint mixes. The check runs where both types are known, at the enqueue, in a
binary that mounts the job. At startup the dispatching binary compares a Pending row's
shape, so a row whose job named a tenant type of another `NAME` is refused there by the
foreign-shape refusal above. That covers the refactor that turns a job module's `use
billing::Org;` into `use crm::Org;`, whenever the two types' NAMEs differ. What a later
binary that mounts the name dispatches unchecked, in the scope type it declares, is a row
whose shape matches:

- a row a hand-written `impl Job` enqueued from a binary that did not mount the job name,
  copying the job's `NAME` and `FINGERPRINT` under another `type Scope`;
- a row enqueued under a tenant type with the same `NAME` as the mounted one. A `NAME` is
  the tenant's identity, so this is the same tenant by declaration: giving a type another
  type's `NAME` declares it that tenant, and one app cannot mount both (§16).

Where the recorded shape matches the mounted one, neither is refused, at startup or at
dispatch. So before a deploy that mounts a scoped job the running binary does not mount,
drain that job: run the binary that enqueued its Pending rows until every one is Done or
Dead, the first way through a shape change below.

There are two ways through a shape change:

- **Drain first.** Run the binary that enqueued them — the old one after an upgrade, the
  newer one after a rollback — until every Pending job of the type is Done or Dead (each
  reaches one within its retry policy), then deploy. In a replicated pair, drain on the
  primary before a switchover onto a follower running another shape, or that follower
  stops as described above.
- **A new type.** Leave the old type's fields alone, put the new fields in a new `#[job]`
  type under a new name, mount both, and switch enqueues to the new one. The name is not
  optional: `NAME` is the type's own identifier, and `mount_jobs` panics on two jobs of
  one name. The old type keeps dispatching its rows, because their shape is still its
  own; remove it once none are Pending.

What the fingerprint cannot see, a change inside a type a field holds, is in §12.

### What `#[job]` rejects

Every rejection is a compile error naming the contract and the fix. The first is the
one every job meets once, and the next three are its neighbours:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
`<job>` declares no tenancy — a job says which. Add one of these to its `#[job(…)]`, keeping any arguments it already has: `scoped_by = Org` if it acts inside one tenant (it is enqueued from inside that tenant's scope, and its `run` receives that tenant's `ScopedTx`), or `global` if it belongs to no tenant (the only kind cron can schedule). Neither is the default.
`global` and `scoped_by = <scope>` on one job — a job is one or the other; drop one
`global` given twice — write it once
`scoped_by` given twice — write it once
```

The second every job meets once too, right after the first: a job that names its
tenancy and not what its Dead means ("What a job's Dead means" above). Its
neighbours refuse both stances at once and either one twice:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
`<job>` declares no Dead stance — a job says what its Dead means. Add one of these to its `#[job(…)]`, keeping any arguments it already has: `on_dead` if the app must act when the job's retries run out (the job then has `fn on_dead(self, tx: &mut Tx, dead: Dead<Self>) -> Result<(), JobError>`, whose writes commit with the Dead mark), or `retain_dead` if the Dead row, kept with its last error, is all that should happen. Neither is the default.
`on_dead` and `retain_dead` are two answers to one question — keep the one this job means
`on_dead` given twice — write it once
`retain_dead` given twice — write it once
```

A `scoped_by` job enqueued where no tenant is named — `tx.enqueue` on a bare `Tx`, or
`App::schedule` — is an unsatisfied bound, and rustc prints this note with your job and
scope in place of `<job>` and `<scope>` (§16 shows it rendered):

<!-- pinned -->
```text
`<job>` is a tenant-scoped job (`#[job(scoped_by = <scope>)]`) and a bare `Tx` names no tenant to run it in
enqueue it from inside the tenant it acts in, and it runs in that tenant:
    let mut tx = tx.scope::<<scope>>(scope, ctx)?;
    tx.enqueue(job);
or fan it out from a `cross_tenant` route or job, naming the tenant:
    tx.enqueue_in::<<scope>>(scope, job, cap);
cron (`App::schedule`) enqueues on a bare `Tx`, so it schedules `global` jobs only
```

The rest are about the attribute's syntax and the struct's shape:

```rust,ignore

struct Foo {}
// "a job declares `global` or `scoped_by = <Type>` and one of `on_dead` /

//  with an optional `timeout = \"<n><unit>\"`, in any order — e.g.
//  `#[job(scoped_by = Org, retain_dead, retry(max = 3, backoff = \"10s\"))]`,
//  `#[job(global, cross_tenant, on_dead)]` or `#[job(scoped_by = Org, on_dead,
//  outbound = \"api.stripe.com\", timeout = \"30s\")]`"

// backoff with no unit suffix
#[job(global, retain_dead, retry(max = 3, backoff = "10"))]
struct Bar {}
// "backoff \"10\" has no unit — a job declares `global` or `scoped_by =
//  <Type>` and one of `on_dead` / `retain_dead`, and may add `cross_tenant`,
//  `retry(max = <int>, backoff = \"<n><unit>\")` (unit is one of ms, s, m, h),
//  and `outbound = \"<host>\"` with an optional `timeout = \"<n><unit>\"`, in
//  any order — e.g. `#[job(scoped_by = Org, retain_dead, retry(max = 3,
//  backoff = \"10s\"))]`, `#[job(global, cross_tenant, on_dead)]` or
//  `#[job(scoped_by = Org, on_dead, outbound = \"api.stripe.com\", timeout =
//  \"30s\")]`"

// enums and unions cannot be job payloads
#[job(global, retain_dead)]
enum Baz {
    A,
}
// "#[job] applies to structs — enums and unions cannot be job payloads"
```

## 7. Cron

Cron rides the same kernel loop as HTTP requests and jobs (§5, §6) — a
schedule is a row, and a due tick is one transaction that advances the
schedule and enqueues a job through the exact same path `tx.enqueue` uses:
a recurring enqueuer, inheriting retry and observability for free.

124	### Examples to copy
125	
126	Four compiled examples ship in the `charpente` crate. `examples/api.rs` is
127	the API page this guide opens with, read and never run: its `main` is empty.
128	The other three are each a small batch that prints the report "Reading a

133	- **In your app**, copy one of the three to `tests/sim.rs` and run

137	  `charpente test --sim --master-seed 0x…`; for an example, pass the same flags
138	  after `--` instead: `cargo run -p charpente --example <name> -- --master-seed

142	|---|---|---|
143	| `drawn_inputs` | `examples/drawn_inputs.rs` | bids drawn with `sim.input()` (`between`, `pick`, `shuffle`, `text`), a check that holds for any of them and merges the tail's re-sent answers into its judgement, and a `require` on a key the check marks when it judged something |
