153	### Drawing inputs
154	
155	`sim.input()` is for the inputs a property must hold for: a name, an amount, an
156	order of operations. Each draw comes from a stream of its own, so drawing moves
157	no fault, and the harness records each draw's choice in a sequence it can replay
158	and shrink. The choice is the one the draw used: the stream's raw value reduced
159	into the draw's range, which is the smallest raw value that draws the same
160	value. So a choice and its value are one to one, and two equal values drawn
161	with the same bounds are equal choices.
162	
163	```text
164	let i = sim.input();
165	let qty = i.between("qty", 1, 500);        // inclusive; shrinks toward 1
166	let kind = i.pick("kind", &["a", "b"]);    // shrinks toward the first item
167	i.shuffle("order", &mut ops);              // shrinks toward the given order
168	let note = i.text("note", &["x", "y"], 1, 4);
169	```
170	
171	It is the workload's own script only: a modelled remote keeps its own `Rng`. A
172	drawn input tests how the app handles what its model stand-in returns, never
173	the real model's behaviour. `between` panics when `lo > hi`, and `pick` on an
174	empty slice. `text` panics when `min_words > max_words`, and on an empty
175	`words` when `max_words` is above 0; with a `max_words` of 0 it draws `""`.
176	Each message names the call and the draw, and says which argument to change.
177	
178	When a check fails, its first failure is shrunk to smaller draws that still
179	fail it, and the failure block lists them by name on its `inputs:` line
180	("Shrinking a failure" below).
181	
182	A loop's length decides how well it shrinks. When the length is a drawn count
183	(`let n = i.between("notes", 1, 4);` and then `n` items, the shape of the
184	scaffold's `tests/sim.rs` and `drawn_inputs.rs`), deleting one item leaves the
185	count stale: the loop reads the next item's draws in its place, the draws after
186	the loop shift, and the run usually passes, while lowering the count alone
187	drops the last item instead. So the shrink can keep items a smaller count would
188	drop. The failure still replays and is still the failure it was, but the shrunk
189	run may not be minimal. When the items after the first matter to a failure (a
190	later item, or a draw after the loop, depends on them), draw a "one more?"
191	choice before each item instead, so that deleting an item deletes exactly its
192	draws:
193	
194	```text
195	let mut qtys = Vec::new();
196	while qtys.len() < 6 && *i.pick("more", &[false, true]) {  // shrinks toward stopping
197	    qtys.push(i.between("qty", 1, 500));
198	}
199	```
200	
201	A batch counts, on each check's line, how many distinct inputs its tested runs
202	drew: two runs that drew the same values, under the same names and in the same
203	order, count once.
204	It is a count, never a threshold. A check whose workload draws nothing is named
205	above the check lines, because every one of its runs tested the same scripted
206	case, whatever the faults did ("Reading a batch" below).
207	
208	### Giving up: a skipped run
209	
210	Sooner or later a workload hits a run where the faults are severe enough
211	that it cannot test its claim at all: the database never opened, the write was
212	never acknowledged, every recovery attempt was exhausted, or durable corruption
213	cut the very record the claim was about. That is not a pass —
214	nothing was proven — and it is not a failure either; the harness did exactly
215	what it was told.
216	
217	Say so:
218	
219	```rust
220	use charpente::{Db, DbConfig, Id, Schema, TxError, View, table};
221	use charpente_sim::Sim;
222	use charpente_sim::checks::{boot_through_fallout, durable_corruption_fired, is_fault_fallout};
223	
224	#[table(global)]
225	struct Counter {
226	    id: Id<Counter>,
227	    hits: u64,
228	}
229	
230	fn counter_survives(sim: &mut Sim) -> Result<(), String> {
231	    let schema = || Schema::new().table::<Counter>();
232	    // A boot that meets an injected fault restarts and boots again, as a
233	    // supervised process would: `Db::open`'s contract for an IO failure.
234	    let open = || Db::open(Box::new(sim.disk()), DbConfig::default(), schema());
235	    let Some(mut db) = boot_through_fallout(sim, 8, is_fault_fallout, open)
236	        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?
237	    else {
238	        // Nothing to adjudicate: the disk never let the claim become testable.
239	        sim.give_up("Db::open never booted in 8 boots", "");
240	        return Ok(());
241	    };
242	    let put = db.transact(|tx| {
243	        tx.put(&Counter {
244	            id: Id::from_raw(1),
245	            hits: 1,
246	        });
247	        Ok::<_, std::io::Error>(())
248	    });
249	    match put {
250	        Ok(()) => {}
251	        // An injected fault kept the write from its ack: no claim to check.
252	        // Any other error is the platform's, and fails, as the opens do.
253	        Err(TxError::Io(e)) if is_fault_fallout(&e.to_string()) => {
254	            sim.give_up("the write was never acknowledged, so there is no claim to check", e);
255	            return Ok(());
256	        }
257	        Err(e) => return Err(format!("{e:?}")),
258	    }
259	
260	    sim.restart(); // a crash: unsynced writes tear or vanish
261	    drop(db); // the old handle is dead after restart
262	    let open = || Db::open(Box::new(sim.disk()), DbConfig::default(), schema());
263	    let Some(db) = boot_through_fallout(sim, 8, is_fault_fallout, open)
264	        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?
265	    else {
266	        sim.give_up("the reopen never booted in 8 boots", "");
267	        return Ok(());
268	    };
269	    match db.snapshot().and_then(|snap| snap.get::<Counter>(Id::from_raw(1))) {
270	        Ok(Some(_)) => Ok(()),
271	        // The one loss the platform excuses on a single node, and an excused
272	        // run GIVES UP: the row's durability was not adjudicated, and a pass
273	        // needs a verdict.
274	        Ok(None) if durable_corruption_fired(sim) => {
275	            sim.give_up("durable corruption cut the acked row, so durability was not adjudicated", "");
276	            Ok(())
277	        }
278	        Ok(None) => Err("acked Counter row lost across a crash".to_string()),
279	        Err(e) if is_fault_fallout(&e.to_string()) => {
280	            sim.give_up("the read-back hit fault fallout", e);
281	            Ok(())
282	        }
283	        Err(e) => Err(e.to_string()),
284	    }
285	}
286	```
287	
288	- `sim.give_up(reason, detail)` records the give-up **on the run**, not in
289	  the value you return. That is deliberate: a `Result` can be mapped back to
290	  `Ok(())` by a wrapper before the runner ever sees it, and for a long time
291	  that is exactly what happened — a property could report green having
292	  concluded nothing over most of its runs.
293	- **The reason is fixed text; the detail is this run's own.** `reason` is a
294	  `&'static str` that names the *kind* of give-up and embeds nothing that
295	  varies between runs: no error text, count or seq. A batch groups each
296	  check's skipped runs by reason and counts each group, so a reason with a seq
297	  in it makes every run its own group and the counts say nothing. What varies
298	  goes in `detail` (anything `Display`, such as the fallout error `e`): that one
299	  run's own text, which a batch does not print and `--seed` prints under the
300	  skipped check as `detail:`. A batch gives each reason the seed of its first
301	  run, `(first: --seed 0x…)`, so `charpente test --sim --filter <check> --seed
302	  0x…` replays that run and prints its detail, then a `fired:` line: what
303	  fired in that run, rendered as a failure block's `fired:` line is (less its
304	  own `run:skipped`), the line to reason from about why it gave up. A
305	  constant such as a retry count is fixed text, so it belongs in the reason
306	  (`"Db::open never booted in 8 boots"`), not the detail. A give-up with
307	  nothing to add passes `""`, and an empty detail is none.
308	  `sim.gave_up()` reads the reason and `sim.gave_up_detail()` the detail;
309	  `Outcome::GaveUp` carries both.
310	- First call wins, reason and detail together; later ones are consequences of
311	  the first.
312	- **Give up and stop.** The record is sticky and nothing enforces terminality,
313	  so if you give up inside a retry arm and the loop then goes on to adjudicate,
314	  the run is still reported as skipped and that verdict is thrown away.
315	  `give_up` and the `return`/`break` belong on the same arm. This bites hardest
316	  in a multi-round checker on your own `sim` (`acked_implies_durable`).
317	- A workload that gives up and then returns `Err` is still a **failure**.
318	  Failures outrank give-ups.
319	- It also marks the coverage key `run:skipped` — once per run, not
320	  once per call — so a give-up *rate* is counted like any other sometimes-key,
321	  and it cross-checks the reported count exactly. A run that gives up and
322	  then returns `Err` is counted as failed, so `charpente test --sim` counts
323	  every key it reached, toward `require` and in the JSON's `coverage`, except
324	  its `run:skipped`. `ceiling:
325	  [("run:skipped", N)]` on `run_universes_swarm!`/`run_universes_swarm_with!`
326	  caps it: the batch fails when more than N runs gave up, naming the key,
327	  the count and the cap. Twenty of the platform's own swarm properties carry
328	  one:
329	  - kernel's exactly-once and job-tenancy properties;
330	  - the flagship properties of tenant, transactions, http, group_commit and
331	    typed_tables, and archive's two convergence properties;
332	  - realtime's flagship, scoped settled-client and tenant-feed properties,
333	    migrations' two, and the WAL suite's fault-matrix, bit-flip, misdirected-write, read-error,
334	    dir-entry and gc properties.
335	
336	  The rest carry none yet, so a drift in their give-up rates is visible only in
337	  the split: realtime's mixed-shapes and follower properties, replication's,
338	  auth's, kernel's job-shape property, transactions' crashed-reseed property,
339	  and engine's. A give-up is
340	  reported and never failed, so without a cap a property can drift toward
341	  adjudicating nothing with every batch green; a floor on the key would bound
342	  give-ups from below, which guards nothing. An app's `sim_tests!` takes no
343	  `ceiling:`. Its property `require`s instead the key its verdict marks, past
344	  every give-up arm. That fails a batch in which no run reached a verdict,
345	  but not one whose rate merely drifted.
346	- A cap bounds what a property fails to conclude, not how much it checks, so
347	  pair it with a `floor: [("key", N)]` on the key that counts its checks
348	  (written before `ceiling:`, on either macro). A change that skips a round's
349	  work without giving up meets every cap. At a pinned base the floor is the
350	  exact count; at an ambient one it is a margin, the mean over ten or more
351	  fresh batches less four standard deviations (§8).
352	- If your workload already funnels give-ups through a wrapper (the
353	  `Err("universe-inconclusive: …")` idiom the platform's own suites use), put
354	  the `sim.give_up(INCONCLUSIVE, e)` call there, beside the `sim.cover(...)` mark. Keep
355	  both: the coverage keys are a floorable distribution over *causes*, and the
356	  outcome is the scalar the runner reports. Neither replaces the other.
357	
358	Every batch states, check by check, how many runs tested the check and, when any
359	were skipped, how many and why. A check with nothing skipped shows no skipped
360	count and is left out of the reasons block, and a batch that skipped nothing
361	prints no reasons block at all. This is a pinned batch of `crates/sim-fixture`,
362	`charpente test --sim --runs 64 --master-seed 0x5eed --filter counter_roundtrip`:
363	
364	<!-- pinned -->
365	```text
366	skipped runs hit a fault before reaching the check, so they prove nothing either way:
367	  counter_roundtrip
368	    10  Db::open after the crash never booted in 8 boots (first: --seed 0x553274161bbf8475)
369	     2  the write was never acked, so durability has nothing to prove (first: --seed 0x70d29b6c7d22528d)
370	
371	these checks draw no inputs, so every run tested the same case — draw them with sim.input() (GUIDE §8):
372	  counter_roundtrip
373	
374	check counter_roundtrip ... ok  (52 tested, 12 skipped)
375	
376	sim result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed. Runs tested: 52 of 64.
377	rerun exactly this batch: charpente test --sim --master-seed 0x5eed --runs 64 --filter counter_roundtrip
378	```
379	
380	A check in which every run was skipped is `untested`, never `ok`, because a
381	property that adjudicated nothing is vacuous no matter how green it looks, and
382	an untested check fails the batch. The batch exits 1, the same as for a failed
383	run, including when `--filter` narrowed it to that one check. Its result line
384	says `FAILED`, or `nothing tested` when no check was tested at all. A line
385	after the skipped runs' reasons names the fixes: raise `--runs`, change the
386	setup until runs reach the check, or delete the check. A run count small enough
387	for every run of a check to be skipped, `--runs 1` while iterating for one,
388	fails the same way. A `--seed` replay of a skipped run is not a batch: it
389	prints the run's reason and detail, and exits 0. This is the harness's own
390	fixture pair, a check that passes and one that always gives up, over six runs:
391	
392	```text
393	skipped runs hit a fault before reaching the check, so they prove nothing either way:
394	  always_gives_up — never tested: every run was skipped
395	    6  the fixture always gives up (first: --seed 0x3071c63893f2dcbd)
396	a check that tested nothing proves nothing, so the batch fails: the reasons above say where its runs stopped. Raise --runs, change the setup until runs reach the check (charpente_sim::drive runs the faulted phase, the recovery and the re-sends), or delete the check.
397	
398	these checks draw no inputs, so every run tested the same case — draw them with sim.input() (GUIDE §8):
399	  always_passes
400	
401	check always_passes ..... ok  (6 tested)
402	check always_gives_up ... untested  (0 tested, 6 skipped)
403	
404	sim result: FAILED. 1 passed; 0 failed; 1 untested. Runs tested per check, in the order above: 6, 0 of 6.
405	rerun exactly this batch: charpente test --sim --master-seed 0x1234 --runs 6
406	```
407	
408	"Reading a batch" below describes each line.
409	
410	**Where the split is visible, and where it is not.** `charpente test --sim`
411	always prints it: the sim binary is `harness = false`, so nothing captures its
412	output. The platform's own internal suites print a line of their own —
413	
414	```text
415	charpente-sim [replication]: 38 of 128 universes reached a verdict, 90 gave up
416	```
417	
418	— but that one goes to stderr from inside a libtest `#[test]`, so **a passing
419	`cargo test` swallows it.** Add `-- --nocapture` to see it (a failing test
420	shows it either way). So do not expect a CI run to surface give-ups; go
421	looking for them. The one exception is a test in which every universe gave up,
422	which fails, as an untested check fails a batch:
423	
424	```text
425	charpente-sim [wal]: every universe gave up, so this test adjudicated nothing over 64 universes and fails. Raise its universe count, or change the workload until universes reach a verdict.
426	```
427	
428	A `CHARPENTE_SEED` replay of one universe that gave up still passes, as a
429	`--seed` replay of a skipped run exits 0.
430	
431	Read that example line the right way round: **38** of those 128 runs
432	adjudicated the property and **90** did not. It is a real measurement from
433	`wal_corruption_on_the_primary_no_longer_loses_acked_records_with_a_follower`,
434	and it means 70% of that property's runs prove nothing — which was
435	invisible before the split was printed, and is the entire reason it is.
436	
437	### A fault-free tail for an end-of-run check
438	
439	A recovery under faults is four steps, and `charpente_sim::drive` runs them.
440	The app supplies how it builds itself on the run's sim and what to send;
441	"Driving the whole app in a sim" below has a compiled workload built on it.
442	
443	```text
444	let drive = Drive::new(sim, build_app); // build_app: Fn(&Sim) -> io::Result<App>
445	let phase = drive.faulted_phase(&requests, Duration::from_secs(2))?; // steps 1 and 2
446	calm.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed); // a remote model's own switch stays yours
447	let Some(recovered) = drive.recover(&phase, Duration::from_secs(60))? else {
448	    return Ok(()); // given up by name
449	}; // steps 3 and 4
450	let snap = recovered.kernel.app().db().snapshot().map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
451	```
452	
453	1. **Boot through fallout.** `faulted_phase` boots the app with
454	   `boot_through_fallout` (below), up to eight boots, restarting between
455	   them as a supervisor would. A first boot that never gets past fault
456	   fallout is no give-up: the phase is empty, and `recover` sends
457	   everything. In every step, fault fallout means `is_fault_fallout(t) ||
458	   clock_fallout(sim, t)`.
459	2. **A faulted phase.** The requests, each an offset from the instant the app
460	   booted and in arrival order, run through one kernel under the run's faults
461	   until nothing is left inside the horizon. An offset past the horizon
462	   panics before anything runs, since the phase would never send that
463	   request, naming the last offset, the horizon and the fix: raise the
464	   horizon past the last request, or space the requests closer. An offset
465	   equal to the horizon is sent. The kernel gets the sim's
466	   outbound handle exactly when the app declares hosts. Fault fallout ends
467	   the phase: it is the crash under test, never a give-up and never a skip,
468	   and the answers already recorded stand. `phase.answers[i]` is request
469	   `i`'s `(status, body)`, or `None` when it went unanswered;
470	   `phase.status(i)` is its status.
471	3. **A tail free of per-call faults; a drawn provider outage runs to its
472	   end.** `recover` power-cycles (`sim.restart()`), quiesces the disk and
473	   clock faults, and the outbound faults when the app declares hosts. A drawn
474	   `outbound_outage` is not a roll, so it refuses its host until its own end.
475	   It waits out a clock refusal, boots, and runs the kernel to `tail` past the
476	   instant it booted, so due jobs, retries and cron drain, then on until the
477	   app's outbound work settles (below). A remote model's own switches, such
478	   as `modelled_remote`'s `calm`, stay in your code: flip them between the two
479	   calls.
480	4. **Re-send what went unanswered.** Every request whose answer is `None`,
481	   or a 5xx whose body is fault fallout, is sent again at the tail's start. A
482	   4xx, or a handler's own 5xx, is the app's answer and is not re-sent.
483	   Fallout is read from the body's text (`is_fault_fallout`), so a handler's
484	   own 5xx whose message reads as fallout ("injected", say) is re-sent too.
485	   The re-sent answers come back in `recovered.resent`, apart from the
486	   phase's, because a request that went unanswered may or may not have
487	   landed. So a claim about acked requests reads `phase.status(i) ==
488	   Some(200)`, and a check that wants the two merged merges them itself
489	   (`examples/drawn_inputs.rs`). A re-sent request lands after everything the
490	   faulted phase ran, not at its offset, so work its offset came before may
491	   already have run by then: a cancel drawn ahead of a reminder's due time
492	   that went unanswered can land after the reminder was sent. A check that
493	   judges when a request took effect treats a re-sent one (a `Some` in
494	   `recovered.resent`) as landing after the phase, since `Recovered` gives no
495	   instant for the tail's start.
496	
497	**The tail settles outbound work.** After the run to `tail`, `recover` reads
498	the store and the wall time the kernel judges due times by: the greater of the
499	clock's reading and the kernel's held wall, which the kernel's open seeds from
500	the store's recorded time, so it can sit up to the 60 s clock tolerance above
501	the clock. It stops when every Pending outbound row is not yet due: no attempt
502	made, and a due time after that wall time, as a delayed job (§6) or a re-issue
503	scheduled later is. Any other Pending outbound row extends the tail: the
504	kernel runs again, as far as the most, over those rows, of the row's wait (to
505	its due time; none once it is due) or the drawn outage's remaining length,
506	whichever is longer, plus its job's declared timeout plus 1 s, and the store
507	is read again. Idle virtual time costs a wake-up, so a retry's wait costs at
508	most one extension and so does a drawn outage, however long: through a 4 h
509	outage a `retry(max = 12)` job takes two extensions, not 17 hours of work, and
510	no app sizes `tail` to its retry policy. An `on_dead` hook that enqueues a fresh job
511	on every Dead, or re-issues at once, makes a chain that ends when the outage
512	ends: through a 4 h outage two such chains on the default policy take one
513	extension, and one on `crates/outbound-fixture`'s `ChargeOrder` policy (eight
514	attempts in 63.5 s) takes two. The extensions stop at
515	`charpente_sim::drive::TAIL_SETTLE_CAP`, 256, with work still Pending, and the
516	run fails by name (below). No extension runs past the year 2262: a retry whose
517	doubling backoff grew past it stays Pending, and once one extension has run to
518	that limit the run fails at once, by its own text naming the job's due time
519	(below), rather than at the end of the u64 nanosecond range, where the kernel
520	stops on its daily sweep's overflow. An app with no host has no outbound row,
521	so it is never extended. `recovered.extensions` counts the extensions, and
522	`recovered.wall` is the wall time the tail stopped at, the time to pass
523	`outbound_settles_by_horizon` ("The checkers", below).
524	
525	**Coverage for a Dead path.** Last, `recover` calls `mark_dead_coverage`
526	("The checkers"), which marks `dead:<job>` once per Dead row, whatever the
527	job's stance: `dead:SendReceipt` for a `SendReceipt` job. Require it to hold
528	that the job's Dead path ran, as `crates/outbound-fixture`'s sim does:
529	`orders_charge_once require ["outbound:checked", "outbound-fixture:re-called",
530	"dead:SendReceipt"]`. A batch in which no run takes the job to Dead fails on
531	the key, naming it, so a Dead path that the sim never exercised cannot read
532	as tested. The tail extends only for outbound work, so a pure `on_dead` job
533	whose retries outlast `tail` is bounded by `tail` as before: size `tail` to
534	its policy before you require its `dead:` key. An outbound job on the default
535	policy reaches Dead under the outage axis, which `charpente test --sim` draws
536	in a quarter of runs, half
537	of them long enough to exhaust the policy ("The outside world: remote
538	models", below), but only where its calls land inside the window. The window
539	opens in the first two seconds of virtual time, so a job called at once is
540	often answered before it opens: the fixture enqueues its receipt 2 s after the
541	order (`enqueue_after`), and measured `dead:SendReceipt` in 486 of 4096 runs,
542	against 35 of 500 when the receipt was sent at once. Measure a required key's
543	rate before you rely on it, and write the rate beside the `require`, as the
544	fixture does: a fresh `cargo test` batch is 256 runs.
545	
546	**A route the tail re-sends must be safe to receive twice.** `Drive`
547	re-sends, and a request that went unanswered may have landed, so its re-send
548	is the second delivery a production client's retry makes. Answer a repeat of
549	the same request with what the first one did, and change nothing:
550	`modelled_remote`'s `place_order` answers an order that is already stored, and
551	the scaffold's `add_note` a note already stored with the same body. A request
552	that reuses the id with other content is a
553	conflict, not a repeat: refuse it with a 4xx that names the conflict and the
554	fix, as `add_note` does for a note that already holds another body. Judge
555	the answers, not only the end state: a guard whose `==` is turned into `!=`
556	refuses the retry and answers the conflict as added, and leaves the store as
557	it was, so the scaffold's three end-state checks pass it. Its fourth,
558	`a_resent_note_changes_nothing_and_a_conflict_is_refused`, posts one note
559	twice with one body and once with another and judges each answer. Key a
560	state transition (a pickup, a cancel) by an id of its own, such as `PUT
561	/pickups/:pickup_id` naming the hold in its body and stored as a row: under
562	`POST /holds/:id/pickup` a retry of a pickup that landed and a fresh pickup of
563	a hold already picked up are the same bytes, while with its own id a repeat
564	finds its row and answers alike and a new pickup of a hold no longer waiting
565	is refused. A route
566	that fails this is an app defect the re-send found, and its check goes red
567	with a seed. Fix the route: dropping below the helper to skip the re-send
568	hides the defect.
569	
570	**Seed fixtures in the build closure, not in the phase.** A `Drive` phase is a
571	fixed request list, so a key one request mints cannot feed a later one, and
572	every setup request sent ahead of a claim's own writes pushes them later into
573	the faulted phase, where fewer get acked and more runs give up: so write the
574	fixtures (an `ApiKey` row in §5's storage form, whose raw key the requests
575	present, and the rows a claim only reads) in the closure `Drive::new` takes,
576	through `App::transact_for_tests`, each only when it is absent, since the
577	closure runs on every boot.
578	
579	`recover` gives `Ok(None)` when the run gave up by name, on a boot refused for
580	durable corruption and on nothing else. Return `Ok(())` then. Its errors fail
581	the run:
582	
583	- `the fault-free tail could not boot`: every boot met fault fallout, and
584	  nothing gave the run up.
585	- `the boot was refused for the clock a third time, after two waits past the
586	  instant each refusal named. …, so this is a platform clock defect, not the
587	  app's: report it with this run's seed. The third refusal: the fault-free tail
588	  could not boot: <refusal>`, from `wait_out_clock_refusal`. One wait always
589	  suffices, so a refusal that outlasts two is a charpente defect, and the run
590	  fails on it rather than hiding it as a skip.
591	- `the fault-free tail could not boot: <error>`: a boot, or the kernel's
592	  build, failed with an error of its own.
593	- `the fault-free tail's kernel stopped: <error>`, in the kernel's words.
594	- `the app calls <host>, but the workload registered no model for it — call
595	  sim.remote("<host>", …) before Drive::faulted_phase`, from either call.
596	- The cap: the tail ran 256 extensions, and an outbound job is still Pending
597	  and due. The text names the first such job by id:
598	
599	<!-- pinned -->
600	```text
601	Drive::recover: the tail ran 256 extensions past its horizon and outbound job <id> ("<name>") is still Pending at attempt <a> — an outbound job settles, retries to Dead, or waits for a later due time; this one did none of them within the cap of 256, so fix the model of the host it calls, or give the job, and the chain its on_dead hook makes, a retry policy that ends
602	```
603	
604	A drawn outage costs one extension however long it lasts, so the outage is
605	never what reaches the cap. A job still retrying after 256 extensions has a
606	remote that never answers it in time and a policy that has not run out (a model
607	that never answers, or a `max` in the thousands), or an `on_dead` hook that
608	starts a new link on every Dead against such a remote, so the chain never
609	ends. Fix the model, or give the job, and the chain its hook makes, a policy
610	that ends. A named job at attempt 0 was due and never dispatched, so it is a
611	row the kernel lost, not the app's: report it with the run's seed.
612	
613	- The limit: an extension has run to the year 2262, its reach meeting or
614	  passing the limit, and an outbound job is still Pending and due. The text
615	  names the job due last and its due time, and comes before the cap:
616	
617	<!-- pinned -->
618	```text
619	Drive::recover: outbound job <id> ("<name>") is still Pending at attempt <a>, due <due>, and the tail ran <n> extension<s>, the last to the year 2262, past which it does not run — a due time that far out means the job's retry backoff grew past the year 2262, so no run reaches its next attempt; give the job a retry policy that ends, a retry(max = …) small enough that it reaches Dead
620	```
621	
622	**When to drop below the helper.** `Drive` is one faulted phase and one tail.
623	A workload with more than that builds it from the pieces this section and
624	"Driving the whole app in a sim" describe: `boot_through_fallout`,
625	`Kernel::new` or `Kernel::with_outbound` over a `SimSource`, the quiesce calls
626	below and `wait_out_clock_refusal`. Examples are several faulted rounds, a
627	supervisor loop inside the phase, a script that reads one phase's answers to
628	build the next, several nodes, a check between the phase and the tail, and a
629	check that reads the frames an SSE subscriber received (`source.sinks()`):
630	`Drive` hands back neither phase's source, so it exposes no frames. §11's
631	"Testing a tail in sim" builds its source by hand to read them. A route that
632	cannot take the re-send is not a reason to drop below it: fix the route
633	(above). Keep each step's rule as `Drive` has it:
634	- use the fallout filter in every step;
635	- treat a crash in the faulted phase as the crash under test, not a skip;
636	- quiesce before the tail boots, and wait out a clock refusal;
637	- give up only on a durable refusal;
638	- re-send in the tail what went unanswered, to routes safe to receive twice.
639	
640	A check that runs at the end of a run — a checkpoint, a graceful close, a
641	byte comparison of two nodes' files — does IO, and the run's
642	`FaultConfig` still applies to it. "No fault has fired so far" is a fact about
643	the past: the check's own fsync can still draw an injected failure. Call
644	`sim.quiesce_disk_faults()` first. For the rest of the run, on every disk,
645	it disarms any pending crash countdown, and no injected read, write, sync or
646	directory-barrier error, misdirected write or restart bit flip fires after it.
647	Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls it
648	replays exactly as before. After it, an error in the check is a real failure,
649	not fallout to classify. Network and object-store faults are untouched, and a
650	restart still power-cycles: unsynced writes and directory entries collapse under
651	the crash model as usual (`crash_apply`, `crash_torn`, `dir_entry_loss`).
652	
653	An outbound workload's tail needs the outbound half as well: the tail is free
654	of per-call faults, and a drawn provider outage runs to its end.
655	`sim.quiesce_outbound_faults()` ends the five outbound fault axes for the rest
656	of the run: no call started after it is refused, lost, throttled or slowed, or
657	loses its reply by chance. A drawn `outbound_outage` is not a roll and runs to
658	its own end, so calls to its host are refused after the quiesce until then.
659	Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls it replays exactly
660	as before. Latency stays, since it is not a fault, and a request already in
661	flight keeps the fate it drew. Call both, then run until the outbound work
662	settles. Outside an outage's window every call reaches its remote and its
663	reply comes back, so an outbound job that is due settles or retries to Dead,
664	and inside one its calls are refused until its retries run out or the window
665	ends. `Drive::recover` runs on until then, at most 256 extensions past
666	`tail` ("The tail settles outbound work", above). A hand driver runs its tail
667	past the last backoff and deadline of every job, and of every chain its
668	`on_dead` hooks make, or loops as `recover` does. Then
669	`outbound_settles_by_horizon(snap, at)` (below) checks that every outbound job
670	due at `at`, the wall time the tail ended at, is Done or Dead, and
671	`mark_dead_coverage` marks the Dead rows' `dead:<job>` keys. A hand driver
672	reads `at` with `sim.clock().wall()` after its last run, and calls
673	`mark_dead_coverage(sim, kernel.app())` itself. Read from the clock, `at` can
674	sit below the wall the kernel holds, by up to the 60 s clock tolerance, when
675	the tail opened over a store whose recorded time was ahead of the clock (after
676	a clock refusal was waited out) and virtual time did not pass it, so a lost
677	row due in that gap passes. `Drive::recover` judges at the greater of the two.
678	
679	A realtime workload's settle phase has the same need for a different fault. The
680	subscriber-stall rate is the one fault axis the sim does not inject itself: a
681	workload reads `sim.subscriber_stall()` and drives its own sink's stall closure
682	at that rate. `sim.quiesce_subscriber_stalls()` makes that accessor read 0.0 for
683	the rest of the run, so a stall closure built after it never refuses a send
684	and draws nothing. Call it before a phase whose verdict rests on a delivery
685	completing. A stall there is a fault the property excuses, so a stall that drops
686	the only clean attempt's tail leaves the run with no verdict at all.
687	
688	A tail that opens a kernel needs the clock half too.
689	`sim.quiesce_clock_faults()` ends the clock faults ("Wall time and its faults",
690	below) for the rest of the run, on every clock. No reading steps back and
691	no power cycle jumps a clock forward after it, so each clock's offset stays
692	where the run left it, skew included. Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a
693	run that never calls it replays exactly as before. It does not undo the
694	past: a step back in an earlier phase can leave the clock more than the
695	tolerance behind the latest time the store recorded, and then the tail's open is
696	refused (§7). With the offset frozen, the clock reaches the instant the refusal
697	names as virtual time passes. `clock_reopens_after(text)` (below) reads that
698	instant. Sleep a little past it (`sim.clock().sleep(…)`), restart the process (a
699	refused node exits, and its supervisor starts it again), and boot again. One
700	wait is enough, since nothing moves the clock or the recorded time in between.
701	Bound the loop anyway, and fail the run by name once the bound is spent: no
702	injected fault explains a refusal one wait did not clear, so it is a platform
703	defect, and a skip would hide it. `wait_out_clock_refusal(sim, boot)` (below)
704	is that loop, and `Drive::recover` runs it around the tail's boot.
705	
706	### Restarting the process, not the machine
707	
708	`sim.restart()` is a power cycle: every unsynced write survives, tears or
709	vanishes before anything reopens. Most restarts in production are not that. A
710	supervisor restarting a crashed, killed or exited process finds the OS page
711	cache intact: every write the dead process made is still readable, synced or
712	not. `sim.restart_process()` models that. Every open file handle dies, exactly
713	as after `restart`, and nothing else happens. Unsynced writes and directory
714	entries stay pending and readable, and the next `restart()` still collapses
715	them.
716	
717	The difference matters because readable is not durable. A node that reads back
718	what a dead process wrote and persists anything derived from it, before making
719	it durable, has built on data the next power loss can take away. A store
720	outran its own log exactly that way: recovery replayed a WAL frame whose fsync
721	had failed, the store checkpointed past it, and a power cycle dropped the frame.
722

content.content:
had failed, the store checkpointed past it, and a power cycle dropped the frame.
Charpente now syncs what it reads back at boot before it acts on it. A property
that only ever power-cycles cannot reach that shape. One that mixes the two can.

The sim's kernel is an honest one: a failed sync leaves its writes pending, and
the next sync writes them. On Linux a failed fsync can instead mark the pages
clean, so the bytes stay readable and never reach the disk. No restart mode
models that, and no later sync can repair it.

Call `restart_process()` before you drop the old process's `Db` to model a kill:
its open files are dead, so nothing it flushes through them on the way out
reaches the disk. Only file handles are gated. A destructor that opens a file
afresh through a `Disk` it still holds would reach the disk; charpente's own
close goes through its open files. Call it after the drop to model an exit.

`sim.unsynced_files()` lists the files that hold writes no sync has taken yet.
Read it right after `restart_process()` to prove the restart left the next
process something unsynced to read back. A property that marks "read back an
unsynced write" from that list cannot be satisfied by a restart that quietly
flushed.

`restart_process()` draws from no random stream and clears no crash countdown,
so the sim gained it without re-keying anyone's runs. Calling it does
change everything your workload does afterwards, as any restart would. It marks
`restart:process`, never `restart`. A crashed disk is power loss, and
`restart_process()` refuses it by name: call `restart()` there. It covers the
global disk; hosts have no process restart.

### Wall time and its faults

A workload reads two times. `sim.now()` is virtual time, the one dimension every
host shares; `SimSource` horizons and `push_at` times are on it. A clock's
`wall()` (`sim.clock()`, or a host's `host.clock()`) is the wall time a node
sees: `sim.true_wall()` (virtual time plus 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z) plus that
clock's offset. `charpente test --sim` puts three faults on the offset, each on
in a quarter of runs, from its own stream:

| Axis (`FaultConfig` field) | What it does | Coverage key |
|---|---|---|
| `clock_skew` | the run's largest skew, up to 120 s: each clock draws its own skew once, uniform within ±`clock_skew`, and reads that far ahead (+) or behind (-) of true time | `clock:skewed`, once per clock, at its first read |
| `clock_step_back` | per wall read, the chance the clock steps back by up to 120 s, and stays there | `clock:stepped-back` per step, and `clock:stepped-back:within-tolerance` or `clock:stepped-back:beyond-tolerance` by its size against `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` |
| `clock_downtime` | per power cycle (`sim.restart()`, `host.restart()`), the chance the clock jumps forward by up to three days, as if the machine had been off; virtual time stays put, and `restart_process()` is not downtime | `clock:downtime`, per jump, at the first reading that shows it |

Each clock's skew, step-backs and jumps are its own, so two hosts' clocks
disagree from their first read. The faults compound. A clock's offset is its
skew plus every step back and jump it has taken so far, and nothing pulls it
back toward true time, just as a clock with no NTP keeps its error, so the
offset wanders further as a run goes on. `sim.clock().offset()` (or
`host.clock().offset()`) reports it at any moment and draws nothing.
The sizes span both sides of `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` (60 s), so a run sees what a node
does with a bad clock (§5, §7): it holds its wall reading at the latest time it
used for a step back within the tolerance, stops by name for one beyond it
(`clock went backwards: …`) or for a hold that lasts longer than the tolerance
(`clock stalled: …`), and refuses to open while its clock is more than the
tolerance behind the latest time its data directory recorded (`refusing to
open: this node's wall clock …`). `clock_refused` names the stops and the
refusal (below). They are fallout only where a clock fault acted:
`clock_fallout(sim, text)` excuses one once a clock in this run has read with
its own skew, stepped back, or shown a jump, and `is_fault_fallout` alone never
does. A node whose clock is right is refused only by a bug, and the platform's
suites run with the clock axes off, so a refusal there fails. An app workload's
filter is `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`. The fault-free
tail above quiesces the clock and then waits out a refusal.

A property that judges expiry and lateness judges two things. Against each
node's own clock readings it holds the node to what it promises (below), which
is exact. Against `sim.true_wall()` it states what that promise means in true
time, written through each clock's offset, since a skewed clock is the thing
under test and a bound that assumes the node's reading is true time fails on
correct code. The platform's own suites (`run_universes_swarm!`, `Sim::new`,
`FaultConfig::default()` and `none()`) leave the three axes off; a platform
property turns them on in `run_universes_swarm_with!`'s `adjust`, which is
handed the run's seed with its config (`|seed, cfg| …`), so any value it
draws comes from a stream keyed by that seed.

`tests/clock.rs` in the `charpente` crate (`crates/charpente/tests/clock.rs` in
a checkout) is the worked example. It runs four platform properties with all
three axes on (sessions, a one-second schedule, retries, and the stops and
refusals themselves, on one node and on a follower promoted on its own host's
clock) and a victim clock that fails two of them by name. It shows how to write
the bounds.

Write a bound through each clock's offset, the reading minus `sim.true_wall()`
at that instant, never through `clock_skew`. A step back within the tolerance
is held and then caught up, so step-backs add up, and a clock can run any
distance behind true time without a check firing. A bound on `expires_at` that
allows only the skew fails on correct code.

What a node does guarantee is relative to its own clock. The time it hands out
is never behind its clock's reading, and never more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE`
ahead of it: the hold takes the larger, the stop fires past the tolerance, and
the open refuses past it. Nor does it stay ahead for longer than the tolerance
at a stretch, since the stall stop ends the hold. That gives these bounds:
- A session resolves only while the clock judging it reads before its
  `expires_at`. In true time, it resolves no later than its TTL plus the
  tolerance after it was minted, plus however far the judging clock has fallen
  behind the minting one.
- A schedule never sits idle once its slot has come on the node's clock.
- Two ticks are never further apart in true time than one interval plus the
  tolerance, plus the clock's own loss and the time the node was busy.

The file records every wall read the kernel makes (a `Clock` wrapper around
`sim.clock()`) and steps the kernel by hand. That ties each response, tick and
retry to the reading it was decided at.

### The checkers

`charpente_sim::checks` ships eighteen functions: thirteen reusable oracles, two
typed event reads, and three idioms, one for a boot and two for a tail that waits out a clock
refusal. Reach for these before hand-rolling the same logic a fourth time:

- `is_fault_fallout(text: &str) -> bool` — classifies an error's *text*:
  is this the harness's own injected fault (or its consequences) rather
  than a bug your workload should fail on? It recognizes the sim's
  injected-fault wording (including the `read_error` axis), the WAL/engine
  poison wording, and redb's "close and re-open the database" latch. Used
  inside a workload to turn "the disk broke, as instructed" into "no answer
  this round" rather than a hard failure — never to swallow anything else.
  (`misdirected_write` is not in that list and cannot be: it returns `Ok`, so
  it has no wording — what you eventually see is the corrupt frame it left
  behind.) **It never excuses the WAL's durable-horizon refusal**, the boot
  refused because an already-acknowledged frame failed its check at or below
  the store's horizon. That refusal is fallout where `bit_flip` or
  `misdirected_write` fired, and a durability bug in the platform everywhere
  else (a real one showed itself only as this refusal in 8 of 21 failing
  bases), and text cannot say which. So it is `false` here, and an open site
  asks `durable_refusal` (below) first, or, for one node of several,
  `SimHost::durable_corruption_fired()`. `boot_through_fallout` does that for
  you. **Nor does it excuse the kernel's clock stops or open/promote refusal**,
  for the same reason: a clock fault or a platform bug produces it, and
  `clock_fallout` (below) tells them apart.
- `classify(text: &str) -> FaultReason` — the families, typed:
  `Injected`, `Poisoned`, `RedbLatch`, `DurableHorizon`, `ClockRefused`, or
  `Unrelated` (`is_fault_fallout` is `Injected | Poisoned | RedbLatch`). Use it when your
  workload wants to accept some families and fail on others — e.g. "an
  injected fault is fallout this round, but a poisoned engine is a finding" —
  or to name the family in a coverage key. `DurableHorizon` and
  `ClockRefused` are names, never excuses on their own. Matching on a variant instead of on substrings keeps
  the prose coupling in one place: if a platform error string is ever
  reworded, `classify` is the single site that must change, and it fails by
  name instead of leaking a wrong classification into whichever oracle saw
  the text first.
- `clock_refused(text: &str) -> bool` — true for the kernel's clock stops
  (`clock went backwards: …`, `clock stalled: …`) and for its refusal to open or promote a node
  whose wall clock is more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` behind the latest time its
  data directory recorded (`refusing to open: this node's wall clock …`,
  `refusing to promote: this node's wall clock …`). A name only: the clock
  axes produce both ("Wall time and its faults", above), and so does a
  platform bug that refuses a node whose clock is right.
- `clock_fallout(sim: &Sim, text: &str) -> bool` — the excuse for those:
  true when `clock_refused(text)` holds and a clock fault acted in this run (a
  clock read with its own skew, stepped back, or showed a downtime jump: its
  `clock:*` coverage key fired). Where no clock fault acted, nothing excuses
  the stops or the refusal. An app workload that runs a kernel filters fallout
  with `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`; a workload that
  never builds a kernel cannot see either text.
- `clock_reopens_after(text: &str) -> Option<WallTime>` — the instant a clock
  stop or refusal names as the one after which the node runs again (its final
  "after <instant>", to the millisecond), or `None` for any other text. A
  fault-free tail sleeps a little past it after `sim.quiesce_clock_faults()`,
  restarts the process and boots again ("A fault-free tail", above). The stall
  stop names no instant, so it is `None`: its clock stopped advancing, and no
  wait fixes that. A quiesced clock still advances, so a tail's kernel never
  stalls, and one that does is reported rather than waited out.
- `wait_out_clock_refusal(sim: &Sim, boot: impl FnMut() -> Result<Option<T>, String>) -> Result<Option<T>, String>`
  — that wait, as a loop. It calls `boot` (your boot and kernel, returning
  `Ok(Some(_))` once booted, `Ok(None)` when it gave the run up, and the error's
  text otherwise) and returns what it returns, unless the error is a clock stop
  or refusal that `clock_fallout` excuses and that names an instant. Then it
  sleeps one second past that instant, restarts the process, and calls `boot`
  again, twice at most: a third refusal is an `Err` that fails the run, `the
  boot was refused for the clock a third time, … a platform clock defect, not
  the app's: report it with this run's seed. The third refusal: <refusal>`,
  and never a give-up. Any other error, the stall stop included, comes back
  unchanged. Call it after `sim.quiesce_clock_faults()`; `Drive::recover`
  runs it around the tail's boot, so only a workload below the helper calls
  it.
- `replays_identically(seed: u64, workload: impl Fn(&mut Sim) -> Result<T, String>) -> Result<(), String>`
  — the determinism oracle. Runs `workload` twice, each on its own fresh
  `Sim::new(seed)`, and fails if the returned value or the durable
  end-state (`Sim::durable_fingerprint`) diverge. It always constructs
  plain `Sim::new` worlds — never a *swarm* `FaultConfig` (swarm testing:
  the harness samples each run's fault rates and latency ranges from
  its own seed, so a batch explores many fault mixes instead of every
  run sharing one fixed matrix) — so it re-runs the workload's logic
  under default fault rates rather than replaying the exact fault schedule
  of the swarm run that called it. **It takes a seed because it needs two
  worlds identical at time zero**, which a sim that has already run cannot give
  it — the opposite of the checker below, and the rule is: a checker that needs
  a FRESH world takes a seed, one that continues THIS world takes `&mut Sim`.
- `acked_implies_durable(sim: &mut Sim, rounds: u32, drive: impl FnMut(&mut Sim) -> Result<Vec<String>, String>, verify: impl FnMut(&mut Sim, &[String]) -> Result<(), String>) -> Result<(), String>`
  — the ack-durability property, generically: `rounds` times, `drive` does
  one round of work and returns the ids it promised are durable (classifying
  its own faults with `is_fault_fallout`, same as above), the sim restarts,
  and `verify` checks every id acked *so far* survived. A failure names the
  round it broke on. A run where no round acked anything gives the run
  up by name, with the round count as its detail, since no `verify` could
  have failed. **Pass it your own `sim`, not `sim.seed()`** — it restarts
  the world you give it, so `require: ["restart"]` over it fires, the excuse
  helpers below read the same world your workload ran in, and your run's
  fault config actually applies. Until 2026-09-05 it took a seed and built its
  own `Sim::new` world, which silently did none of those three things; if you
  have code calling it with `sim.seed()`, that code was running outside its
  declared fault matrix and crediting coverage nowhere.
- `durable_corruption_fired(sim: &Sim) -> bool` — true when a
  durable-corruption fault (`bit_flip` or `misdirected_write`) actually
  fired in this run. Those axes can corrupt an acked WAL record above
  the store's checkpoint horizon, and recovery then legitimately cuts it
  (an invalid frame is a torn tail unless provably below the horizon — the
  standard WAL convention; the un-checkpointed data had one local copy).
  Route an acked-durability check's *shortfall* through this so the loss is
  excused only in runs where corruption was actually injected — the
  strong oracle stands everywhere else. **An excused run gives up**
  (`sim.give_up(..)` and stop, as `counter_survives` under "Giving up" does):
  the record's durability was not adjudicated, and a pass needs a verdict, so
  an excuse that returns `Ok` without giving up is a vacuous pass. Never use it
  to excuse wrong data or a consistency violation (a cut reverts state to a prefix, which stays
  consistent). Note this is the *single-node* excuse: a workload with a
  converged follower keeps none of it, because a record the primary lost to
  media corruption still lives on the follower. In a multi-node workload,
  ask `SimHost::durable_corruption_fired()` instead. It answers the same
  question for one host's disk, so a refusal on one node is excused only by
  corruption that fired on that node, never by a fault on another. A workload
  that wipes a host's data (a re-seed) reads
  `SimHost::durable_corruption_count()` and `dir_entry_loss_count()` at the
  wipe, and excuses a later refusal only when the count has grown since: the
  wipe deleted every byte an earlier fault touched.
- `boot_through_fallout(sim: &Sim, tries: u32, is_fallout: impl Fn(&str) -> bool, boot: impl FnMut() -> Result<T, E>) -> Result<Option<T>, E>`
  — boots the way a supervised process does: `boot`, and on an error your
  `is_fallout` accepts, boot again, `tries` boots in all. Each retry marks
  `boot:retried`, a retry that boots marks `boot:booted-after-retry` (require
  that one: it proves the retries do more than run), and running out marks
  `boot:exhausted`. A retry after an injected IO error restarts the process
  first (`sim.restart_process()`, so the page cache survives); a retry after a
  crash power-cycles first (`sim.restart()`, when `Sim::disk_crashed` says the
  disk is gone). `Ok(Some(t))` is the first clean boot and `Err(e)` the first
  error that is not fallout, unchanged. A durable-horizon refusal is judged
  before your `is_fallout` sees it, so no classifier of yours can excuse one
  where no durable corruption fired. `Ok(None)` means every boot met
  fallout, and what it means is yours to say: a workload whose only node
  never came up gives up by name (`counter_survives` above), and a round
  restarts and moves on. The one `None` the helper names itself is a boot
  refused for durable corruption at or below the store's horizon
  (`durable_refusal`, next): no restart clears bytes on the disk, so it stops
  at once, marks `boot:durable-refusal` and gives the run up under that
  name. Where no durable corruption fired, the same refusal is a finding and
  comes back as `Err(e)`, unchanged. Use it at every boot, a round
  loop's included: an injected fault inside the table store's open is
  returned by `Db::open` as the error it is, and the next boot opens the same
  file, so a phase that gives up or skips on its first faulted boot throws
  away work a restart would have recovered. A round loop's next round does
  boot again, but the round it skipped is work the property never checks.
- `durable_refusal(sim: &Sim, text: &str) -> Result<bool, String>` — the
  same rule for a loop that boots on its own, such as a final verification's
  reopen loop: call it on each failed boot's error before the fallout check,
  since `is_fault_fallout` turns the refusal down. `Ok(false)`: not
  a durable refusal, carry on. `Ok(true)`: a refusal in a run where
  durable corruption fired, already given up under its own name and marked
  `boot:durable-refusal`, so end the loop. `Err(..)`: a refusal where none
  fired, which nothing excuses, so fail with the text it names. A loop that
  retries a durable refusal spends its whole budget on bytes no restart
  clears, then gives up claiming the attempts all hit injected faults.
- `dir_entry_loss_fired(sim: &Sim) -> bool` — the same fire-time-marked
  discipline for the `dir_entry_loss` axis (a pending directory create
  vanished, or a pending removal resurrected). A workload that routes
  `Db::open`'s "a segment is missing … refusing to guess" to a restore path
  must do so *only* when this returns true: the platform never leaves a
  durable directory gap on its own, so a gap in a run where the axis
  never fired is a real regression and must fail loud. In a multi-node
  workload, ask `SimHost::dir_entry_loss_fired()` instead: it answers for one
  host's disk, so one node's gap is never excused by entry loss on another.
- `calls_have_durable_jobs(sim: &Sim, snap: &Snapshot) -> Result<(), String>` —
  every call that reached a remote (`sim.outbound_deliveries()`) carries the
  key of a job in `snap`, the recovered store, so no call fired for an enqueue
  that never became durable. It attributes a call by `OutboundCall::key`,
  never by where the app put the key in the request. One sim box has one loss
  window, media corruption: a bit flip can cut an acknowledged enqueue whose
  call was already made, and then this check fails. Route a failure through
  `durable_corruption_fired` and give the run up where it fired, never
  pass it, the same rule as any acked-durability shortfall.
- `keys_are_per_effect(snap: &Snapshot) -> Result<(), String>` — a key carries
  exactly one request. Every row that holds one has the same name and the same
  payload bytes, and at most one of them is not Dead: only a re-issue from
  `on_dead` copies a key, together with its request, and the row it copies is Dead
  by then. It fails wherever a key carries two requests, or two jobs that are not
  Dead, which would send the effect twice. The error names both jobs and the key, and what differs.
- `outbound_settles_by_horizon(snap: &Snapshot, at: WallTime) -> Result<(), String>`
  — every outbound job due at `at` is Done or Dead. `at` is the wall time
  the tail ended at: `recovered.wall` after `Drive::recover` (the greater of
  the clock's reading and the kernel's held wall), or `sim.clock().wall()`
  read after a hand driver's last run. A Pending row with
  no attempt made and a due time after `at` is not judged, since it is not yet
  due: a delayed job (§6) or a re-issue scheduled later. Every other Pending
  outbound row fails it, the first by id, as lost by the kernel: one due and
  never attempted, or a retry the tail did not run past. Call it only after
  the tail: `sim.quiesce_disk_faults()`, `sim.quiesce_outbound_faults()`, and
  a run until the outbound work settles ("A fault-free tail", above).
- `mark_dead_coverage(sim: &Sim, app: &App) -> Result<(), String>` — marks
  `dead:<job>` once per Dead row in `app`'s store, whatever the job's stance,
  so a sim can `require:` that a job's Dead path ran. `Drive::recover` calls
  it last. A hand driver calls it once, after the tail, on its last kernel's
  App (`kernel.app()`): the key is the job's `JobDef::dead_coverage`, which
  the App keeps after the kernel takes its job definitions. It reads the
  store and draws nothing, so a run in which nothing goes Dead marks nothing
  and replays as before. A Dead row of a job the App does not mount has no
  key and marks nothing. Its `Err` is a failed read of the store.
- `dead_hooks_succeeded(snap: &Snapshot) -> Result<(), String>` — no `on_dead`
  hook failed (§6, "When the hook fails"). A failed hook's Dead mark commits
  alone, with a `last_error` that begins `charpente: on_dead failed: `, so what
  the hook was to do (tell someone, re-issue the effect) never happened. The
  check reads that prefix from every Dead row in `snap` and fails on the first,
  by id. The prefix is in the row, so it survives the drive's kernel swap and
  every restart, as a counter in memory would not, and an app's own text that
  begins with it is stored behind `job error: `, so app text neither trips the
  check nor hides a failure from it. Call it on the recovered store at the end of
  a run, beside the other end-state checks. A hook's `Err(JobError::App)`, panic
  or refused transaction is the app's own deterministic bug, so a run in which
  one happened fails, and never gives up. A hook's other `Err(JobError::Io)` is
  not a failure: nothing commits, the job runs again, and no prefix is written.
  `charpente new`'s scaffold calls it in its echo property, where it passes
  trivially until a job declares `on_dead`; from then on it fails any run in which
  that hook failed. Its failure names the job and quotes what
  follows the prefix, the hook's error and then the job's (below).
- `events::<E: Event>(snap: &Snapshot) -> Result<Vec<E>, String>` and
  `events_scoped::<E: Event>(snap: &Snapshot, tenant: u64) -> Result<Vec<E>, String>
  where E::Scope: Tenant` — the durable event log read as your own event
  types, in log order: every row named `E::NAME` (for `events_scoped`, only
  those emitted in that tenant's scope, `tenant` being the raw id), decoded.
  `events_scoped` takes only a `#[event(scoped_by = ..)]` type; a global one
  does not compile there. They read every page of the log (`EVENTS_PAGE`
  rows a call), so a long run is read whole. A row is decoded only under the
  shape it was written with: a different fingerprint, a payload that does not
  decode, or bytes left over after it is an `Err` naming the event, the row
  id and the fix (read it with the type that wrote it), never a skipped row.
  Use them instead of scanning `EventRow` and decoding by hand.
