A worked `acked_implies_durable` example — a toy that writes one byte per
round and only claims the ack once its `sync` returns `Ok`:

```rust
use charpente::core::io::Disk;
use charpente_sim::Sim;
use charpente_sim::checks::{acked_implies_durable, is_fault_fallout};

/// Returns a fresh `drive` closure: each call performs one round, writing
/// the next byte and syncing before claiming its ack — never before.
fn drive() -> impl FnMut(&mut Sim) -> Result<Vec<String>, String> {
    let mut round: u64 = 0;
    move |sim: &mut Sim| {
        let file = match sim.disk().open("bytes") {
            Ok(f) => f,
            Err(e) if is_fault_fallout(&e.to_string()) => return Ok(vec![]),
            Err(e) => return Err(e.to_string()),
        };
        if let Err(e) = file.write_at(round, &[0xAA]) {
            let msg = e.to_string();
            return if is_fault_fallout(&msg) { Ok(vec![]) } else { Err(msg) };
        }
        if let Err(e) = file.sync() {
            let msg = e.to_string();
            return if is_fault_fallout(&msg) { Ok(vec![]) } else { Err(msg) };
        }
        let id = format!("byte-{round}");
        round += 1;
        Ok(vec![id])
    }
}

fn verify(sim: &mut Sim, acked: &[String]) -> Result<(), String> {
    let file = sim.disk().open("bytes").map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
    let len = file.len().map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
    for id in acked {
        let offset: u64 = id
            .strip_prefix("byte-")
            .expect("ack ids are \"byte-N\"")
            .parse()
            .expect("ack ids carry a numeric offset");
        if offset >= len {
            return Err(format!("{id} missing after restart (file len {len})"));
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn bytes_survive_restarts(sim: &mut Sim) -> Result<(), String> {
    // `sim`, not `sim.seed()`: the checker restarts the world you hand it, so
    // the `restart` coverage lands where the harness reads it and your
    // run's fault config is the one the property runs under.
    acked_implies_durable(sim, 5, drive(), verify)
}
```

### Driving the whole app in a sim

The workloads above drive `Db` directly. The full app — routes, jobs, and
cron multiplexed on one loop — is just as drivable, because the loop itself

tool_use_result.stdout:
had failed, the store checkpointed past it, and a power cycle dropped the frame.
Charpente now syncs what it reads back at boot before it acts on it. A property
that only ever power-cycles cannot reach that shape. One that mixes the two can.

The sim's kernel is an honest one: a failed sync leaves its writes pending, and
the next sync writes them. On Linux a failed fsync can instead mark the pages
clean, so the bytes stay readable and never reach the disk. No restart mode
models that, and no later sync can repair it.

Call `restart_process()` before you drop the old process's `Db` to model a kill:
its open files are dead, so nothing it flushes through them on the way out
reaches the disk. Only file handles are gated. A destructor that opens a file
afresh through a `Disk` it still holds would reach the disk; charpente's own
close goes through its open files. Call it after the drop to model an exit.

`sim.unsynced_files()` lists the files that hold writes no sync has taken yet.
Read it right after `restart_process()` to prove the restart left the next
process something unsynced to read back. A property that marks "read back an
unsynced write" from that list cannot be satisfied by a restart that quietly
flushed.

`restart_process()` draws from no random stream and clears no crash countdown,
so the sim gained it without re-keying anyone's runs. Calling it does
change everything your workload does afterwards, as any restart would. It marks
`restart:process`, never `restart`. A crashed disk is power loss, and
`restart_process()` refuses it by name: call `restart()` there. It covers the
global disk; hosts have no process restart.

### Wall time and its faults

A workload reads two times. `sim.now()` is virtual time, the one dimension every
host shares; `SimSource` horizons and `push_at` times are on it. A clock's
`wall()` (`sim.clock()`, or a host's `host.clock()`) is the wall time a node
sees: `sim.true_wall()` (virtual time plus 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z) plus that
clock's offset. `charpente test --sim` puts three faults on the offset, each on
in a quarter of runs, from its own stream:

| Axis (`FaultConfig` field) | What it does | Coverage key |
|---|---|---|
| `clock_skew` | the run's largest skew, up to 120 s: each clock draws its own skew once, uniform within ±`clock_skew`, and reads that far ahead (+) or behind (-) of true time | `clock:skewed`, once per clock, at its first read |
| `clock_step_back` | per wall read, the chance the clock steps back by up to 120 s, and stays there | `clock:stepped-back` per step, and `clock:stepped-back:within-tolerance` or `clock:stepped-back:beyond-tolerance` by its size against `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` |
| `clock_downtime` | per power cycle (`sim.restart()`, `host.restart()`), the chance the clock jumps forward by up to three days, as if the machine had been off; virtual time stays put, and `restart_process()` is not downtime | `clock:downtime`, per jump, at the first reading that shows it |

Each clock's skew, step-backs and jumps are its own, so two hosts' clocks
disagree from their first read. The faults compound. A clock's offset is its
skew plus every step back and jump it has taken so far, and nothing pulls it
back toward true time, just as a clock with no NTP keeps its error, so the
offset wanders further as a run goes on. `sim.clock().offset()` (or
`host.clock().offset()`) reports it at any moment and draws nothing.
The sizes span both sides of `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` (60 s), so a run sees what a node
does with a bad clock (§5, §7): it holds its wall reading at the latest time it
used for a step back within the tolerance, stops by name for one beyond it
(`clock went backwards: …`) or for a hold that lasts longer than the tolerance
(`clock stalled: …`), and refuses to open while its clock is more than the
tolerance behind the latest time its data directory recorded (`refusing to
open: this node's wall clock …`). `clock_refused` names the stops and the
refusal (below). They are fallout only where a clock fault acted:
`clock_fallout(sim, text)` excuses one once a clock in this run has read with
its own skew, stepped back, or shown a jump, and `is_fault_fallout` alone never
does. A node whose clock is right is refused only by a bug, and the platform's
suites run with the clock axes off, so a refusal there fails. An app workload's
filter is `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`. The fault-free
tail above quiesces the clock and then waits out a refusal.

A property that judges expiry and lateness judges two things. Against each
node's own clock readings it holds the node to what it promises (below), which
is exact. Against `sim.true_wall()` it states what that promise means in true
time, written through each clock's offset, since a skewed clock is the thing
under test and a bound that assumes the node's reading is true time fails on
correct code. The platform's own suites (`run_universes_swarm!`, `Sim::new`,
`FaultConfig::default()` and `none()`) leave the three axes off; a platform
property turns them on in `run_universes_swarm_with!`'s `adjust`, which is
handed the run's seed with its config (`|seed, cfg| …`), so any value it
draws comes from a stream keyed by that seed.

`tests/clock.rs` in the `charpente` crate (`crates/charpente/tests/clock.rs` in
a checkout) is the worked example. It runs four platform properties with all
three axes on (sessions, a one-second schedule, retries, and the stops and
refusals themselves, on one node and on a follower promoted on its own host's
clock) and a victim clock that fails two of them by name. It shows how to write
the bounds.

Write a bound through each clock's offset, the reading minus `sim.true_wall()`
at that instant, never through `clock_skew`. A step back within the tolerance
is held and then caught up, so step-backs add up, and a clock can run any
distance behind true time without a check firing. A bound on `expires_at` that
allows only the skew fails on correct code.

What a node does guarantee is relative to its own clock. The time it hands out
is never behind its clock's reading, and never more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE`
ahead of it: the hold takes the larger, the stop fires past the tolerance, and
the open refuses past it. Nor does it stay ahead for longer than the tolerance
at a stretch, since the stall stop ends the hold. That gives these bounds:
- A session resolves only while the clock judging it reads before its
  `expires_at`. In true time, it resolves no later than its TTL plus the
  tolerance after it was minted, plus however far the judging clock has fallen
  behind the minting one.
- A schedule never sits idle once its slot has come on the node's clock.
- Two ticks are never further apart in true time than one interval plus the
  tolerance, plus the clock's own loss and the time the node was busy.

The file records every wall read the kernel makes (a `Clock` wrapper around
`sim.clock()`) and steps the kernel by hand. That ties each response, tick and
retry to the reading it was decided at.

### The checkers

`charpente_sim::checks` ships eighteen functions: thirteen reusable oracles, two
typed event reads, and three idioms, one for a boot and two for a tail that waits out a clock
refusal. Reach for these before hand-rolling the same logic a fourth time:

- `is_fault_fallout(text: &str) -> bool` — classifies an error's *text*:
  is this the harness's own injected fault (or its consequences) rather
  than a bug your workload should fail on? It recognizes the sim's
  injected-fault wording (including the `read_error` axis), the WAL/engine
  poison wording, and redb's "close and re-open the database" latch. Used
  inside a workload to turn "the disk broke, as instructed" into "no answer
  this round" rather than a hard failure — never to swallow anything else.
  (`misdirected_write` is not in that list and cannot be: it returns `Ok`, so
  it has no wording — what you eventually see is the corrupt frame it left
  behind.) **It never excuses the WAL's durable-horizon refusal**, the boot
  refused because an already-acknowledged frame failed its check at or below
  the store's horizon. That refusal is fallout where `bit_flip` or
  `misdirected_write` fired, and a durability bug in the platform everywhere
  else (a real one showed itself only as this refusal in 8 of 21 failing
  bases), and text cannot say which. So it is `false` here, and an open site
  asks `durable_refusal` (below) first, or, for one node of several,
  `SimHost::durable_corruption_fired()`. `boot_through_fallout` does that for
  you. **Nor does it excuse the kernel's clock stops or open/promote refusal**,
  for the same reason: a clock fault or a platform bug produces it, and
  `clock_fallout` (below) tells them apart.
- `classify(text: &str) -> FaultReason` — the families, typed:
  `Injected`, `Poisoned`, `RedbLatch`, `DurableHorizon`, `ClockRefused`, or
  `Unrelated` (`is_fault_fallout` is `Injected | Poisoned | RedbLatch`). Use it when your
  workload wants to accept some families and fail on others — e.g. "an
  injected fault is fallout this round, but a poisoned engine is a finding" —
  or to name the family in a coverage key. `DurableHorizon` and
  `ClockRefused` are names, never excuses on their own. Matching on a variant instead of on substrings keeps
  the prose coupling in one place: if a platform error string is ever
  reworded, `classify` is the single site that must change, and it fails by
  name instead of leaking a wrong classification into whichever oracle saw
  the text first.
- `clock_refused(text: &str) -> bool` — true for the kernel's clock stops
  (`clock went backwards: …`, `clock stalled: …`) and for its refusal to open or promote a node
  whose wall clock is more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` behind the latest time its
  data directory recorded (`refusing to open: this node's wall clock …`,
  `refusing to promote: this node's wall clock …`). A name only: the clock
  axes produce both ("Wall time and its faults", above), and so does a
  platform bug that refuses a node whose clock is right.
- `clock_fallout(sim: &Sim, text: &str) -> bool` — the excuse for those:
  true when `clock_refused(text)` holds and a clock fault acted in this run (a
  clock read with its own skew, stepped back, or showed a downtime jump: its
  `clock:*` coverage key fired). Where no clock fault acted, nothing excuses
  the stops or the refusal. An app workload that runs a kernel filters fallout
  with `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`; a workload that
  never builds a kernel cannot see either text.
- `clock_reopens_after(text: &str) -> Option<WallTime>` — the instant a clock
  stop or refusal names as the one after which the node runs again (its final
  "after <instant>", to the millisecond), or `None` for any other text. A
  fault-free tail sleeps a little past it after `sim.quiesce_clock_faults()`,
  restarts the process and boots again ("A fault-free tail", above). The stall
  stop names no instant, so it is `None`: its clock stopped advancing, and no
  wait fixes that. A quiesced clock still advances, so a tail's kernel never
  stalls, and one that does is reported rather than waited out.
- `wait_out_clock_refusal(sim: &Sim, boot: impl FnMut() -> Result<Option<T>, String>) -> Result<Option<T>, String>`
  — that wait, as a loop. It calls `boot` (your boot and kernel, returning
  `Ok(Some(_))` once booted, `Ok(None)` when it gave the run up, and the error's
  text otherwise) and returns what it returns, unless the error is a clock stop
  or refusal that `clock_fallout` excuses and that names an instant. Then it
  sleeps one second past that instant, restarts the process, and calls `boot`
  again, twice at most: a third refusal is an `Err` that fails the run, `the
  boot was refused for the clock a third time, … a platform clock defect, not
  the app's: report it with this run's seed. The third refusal: <refusal>`,
  and never a give-up. Any other error, the stall stop included, comes back
  unchanged. Call it after `sim.quiesce_clock_faults()`; `Drive::recover`
  runs it around the tail's boot, so only a workload below the helper calls
  it.
- `replays_identically(seed: u64, workload: impl Fn(&mut Sim) -> Result<T, String>) -> Result<(), String>`
  — the determinism oracle. Runs `workload` twice, each on its own fresh
  `Sim::new(seed)`, and fails if the returned value or the durable
  end-state (`Sim::durable_fingerprint`) diverge. It always constructs
  plain `Sim::new` worlds — never a *swarm* `FaultConfig` (swarm testing:
  the harness samples each run's fault rates and latency ranges from
  its own seed, so a batch explores many fault mixes instead of every
  run sharing one fixed matrix) — so it re-runs the workload's logic
  under default fault rates rather than replaying the exact fault schedule
  of the swarm run that called it. **It takes a seed because it needs two
  worlds identical at time zero**, which a sim that has already run cannot give
  it — the opposite of the checker below, and the rule is: a checker that needs
  a FRESH world takes a seed, one that continues THIS world takes `&mut Sim`.
- `acked_implies_durable(sim: &mut Sim, rounds: u32, drive: impl FnMut(&mut Sim) -> Result<Vec<String>, String>, verify: impl FnMut(&mut Sim, &[String]) -> Result<(), String>) -> Result<(), String>`
  — the ack-durability property, generically: `rounds` times, `drive` does
  one round of work and returns the ids it promised are durable (classifying
  its own faults with `is_fault_fallout`, same as above), the sim restarts,
  and `verify` checks every id acked *so far* survived. A failure names the
  round it broke on. A run where no round acked anything gives the run
  up by name, with the round count as its detail, since no `verify` could
  have failed. **Pass it your own `sim`, not `sim.seed()`** — it restarts
  the world you give it, so `require: ["restart"]` over it fires, the excuse
  helpers below read the same world your workload ran in, and your run's
  fault config actually applies. Until 2026-09-05 it took a seed and built its
  own `Sim::new` world, which silently did none of those three things; if you
  have code calling it with `sim.seed()`, that code was running outside its
  declared fault matrix and crediting coverage nowhere.
- `durable_corruption_fired(sim: &Sim) -> bool` — true when a
  durable-corruption fault (`bit_flip` or `misdirected_write`) actually
  fired in this run. Those axes can corrupt an acked WAL record above
  the store's checkpoint horizon, and recovery then legitimately cuts it
  (an invalid frame is a torn tail unless provably below the horizon — the
  standard WAL convention; the un-checkpointed data had one local copy).
  Route an acked-durability check's *shortfall* through this so the loss is
  excused only in runs where corruption was actually injected — the
  strong oracle stands everywhere else. **An excused run gives up**
  (`sim.give_up(..)` and stop, as `counter_survives` under "Giving up" does):
  the record's durability was not adjudicated, and a pass needs a verdict, so
  an excuse that returns `Ok` without giving up is a vacuous pass. Never use it
  to excuse wrong data or a consistency violation (a cut reverts state to a prefix, which stays
  consistent). Note this is the *single-node* excuse: a workload with a
  converged follower keeps none of it, because a record the primary lost to
  media corruption still lives on the follower. In a multi-node workload,
  ask `SimHost::durable_corruption_fired()` instead. It answers the same
  question for one host's disk, so a refusal on one node is excused only by
  corruption that fired on that node, never by a fault on another. A workload
  that wipes a host's data (a re-seed) reads
  `SimHost::durable_corruption_count()` and `dir_entry_loss_count()` at the
  wipe, and excuses a later refusal only when the count has grown since: the
  wipe deleted every byte an earlier fault touched.
- `boot_through_fallout(sim: &Sim, tries: u32, is_fallout: impl Fn(&str) -> bool, boot: impl FnMut() -> Result<T, E>) -> Result<Option<T>, E>`
  — boots the way a supervised process does: `boot`, and on an error your
  `is_fallout` accepts, boot again, `tries` boots in all. Each retry marks
  `boot:retried`, a retry that boots marks `boot:booted-after-retry` (require
  that one: it proves the retries do more than run), and running out marks
  `boot:exhausted`. A retry after an injected IO error restarts the process
  first (`sim.restart_process()`, so the page cache survives); a retry after a
  crash power-cycles first (`sim.restart()`, when `Sim::disk_crashed` says the
  disk is gone). `Ok(Some(t))` is the first clean boot and `Err(e)` the first
  error that is not fallout, unchanged. A durable-horizon refusal is judged
  before your `is_fallout` sees it, so no classifier of yours can excuse one
  where no durable corruption fired. `Ok(None)` means every boot met
  fallout, and what it means is yours to say: a workload whose only node
  never came up gives up by name (`counter_survives` above), and a round
  restarts and moves on. The one `None` the helper names itself is a boot
  refused for durable corruption at or below the store's horizon
  (`durable_refusal`, next): no restart clears bytes on the disk, so it stops
  at once, marks `boot:durable-refusal` and gives the run up under that
  name. Where no durable corruption fired, the same refusal is a finding and
  comes back as `Err(e)`, unchanged. Use it at every boot, a round
  loop's included: an injected fault inside the table store's open is
  returned by `Db::open` as the error it is, and the next boot opens the same
  file, so a phase that gives up or skips on its first faulted boot throws
  away work a restart would have recovered. A round loop's next round does
  boot again, but the round it skipped is work the property never checks.
- `durable_refusal(sim: &Sim, text: &str) -> Result<bool, String>` — the
  same rule for a loop that boots on its own, such as a final verification's
  reopen loop: call it on each failed boot's error before the fallout check,
  since `is_fault_fallout` turns the refusal down. `Ok(false)`: not
  a durable refusal, carry on. `Ok(true)`: a refusal in a run where
  durable corruption fired, already given up under its own name and marked
  `boot:durable-refusal`, so end the loop. `Err(..)`: a refusal where none
  fired, which nothing excuses, so fail with the text it names. A loop that
  retries a durable refusal spends its whole budget on bytes no restart
  clears, then gives up claiming the attempts all hit injected faults.
- `dir_entry_loss_fired(sim: &Sim) -> bool` — the same fire-time-marked
  discipline for the `dir_entry_loss` axis (a pending directory create
  vanished, or a pending removal resurrected). A workload that routes
  `Db::open`'s "a segment is missing … refusing to guess" to a restore path
  must do so *only* when this returns true: the platform never leaves a
  durable directory gap on its own, so a gap in a run where the axis
  never fired is a real regression and must fail loud. In a multi-node
  workload, ask `SimHost::dir_entry_loss_fired()` instead: it answers for one
  host's disk, so one node's gap is never excused by entry loss on another.
- `calls_have_durable_jobs(sim: &Sim, snap: &Snapshot) -> Result<(), String>` —
  every call that reached a remote (`sim.outbound_deliveries()`) carries the
  key of a job in `snap`, the recovered store, so no call fired for an enqueue
  that never became durable. It attributes a call by `OutboundCall::key`,
  never by where the app put the key in the request. One sim box has one loss
  window, media corruption: a bit flip can cut an acknowledged enqueue whose
  call was already made, and then this check fails. Route a failure through
  `durable_corruption_fired` and give the run up where it fired, never
  pass it, the same rule as any acked-durability shortfall.
- `keys_are_per_effect(snap: &Snapshot) -> Result<(), String>` — a key carries
  exactly one request. Every row that holds one has the same name and the same
  payload bytes, and at most one of them is not Dead: only a re-issue from
  `on_dead` copies a key, together with its request, and the row it copies is Dead
  by then. It fails wherever a key carries two requests, or two jobs that are not
  Dead, which would send the effect twice. The error names both jobs and the key, and what differs.
- `outbound_settles_by_horizon(snap: &Snapshot, at: WallTime) -> Result<(), String>`
  — every outbound job due at `at` is Done or Dead. `at` is the wall time
  the tail ended at: `recovered.wall` after `Drive::recover` (the greater of
  the clock's reading and the kernel's held wall), or `sim.clock().wall()`
  read after a hand driver's last run. A Pending row with
  no attempt made and a due time after `at` is not judged, since it is not yet
  due: a delayed job (§6) or a re-issue scheduled later. Every other Pending
  outbound row fails it, the first by id, as lost by the kernel: one due and
  never attempted, or a retry the tail did not run past. Call it only after
  the tail: `sim.quiesce_disk_faults()`, `sim.quiesce_outbound_faults()`, and
  a run until the outbound work settles ("A fault-free tail", above).
- `mark_dead_coverage(sim: &Sim, app: &App) -> Result<(), String>` — marks
  `dead:<job>` once per Dead row in `app`'s store, whatever the job's stance,
  so a sim can `require:` that a job's Dead path ran. `Drive::recover` calls
  it last. A hand driver calls it once, after the tail, on its last kernel's
  App (`kernel.app()`): the key is the job's `JobDef::dead_coverage`, which
  the App keeps after the kernel takes its job definitions. It reads the
  store and draws nothing, so a run in which nothing goes Dead marks nothing
  and replays as before. A Dead row of a job the App does not mount has no
  key and marks nothing. Its `Err` is a failed read of the store.
- `dead_hooks_succeeded(snap: &Snapshot) -> Result<(), String>` — no `on_dead`
  hook failed (§6, "When the hook fails"). A failed hook's Dead mark commits
  alone, with a `last_error` that begins `charpente: on_dead failed: `, so what
  the hook was to do (tell someone, re-issue the effect) never happened. The
  check reads that prefix from every Dead row in `snap` and fails on the first,
  by id. The prefix is in the row, so it survives the drive's kernel swap and
  every restart, as a counter in memory would not, and an app's own text that
  begins with it is stored behind `job error: `, so app text neither trips the
  check nor hides a failure from it. Call it on the recovered store at the end of
  a run, beside the other end-state checks. A hook's `Err(JobError::App)`, panic
  or refused transaction is the app's own deterministic bug, so a run in which
  one happened fails, and never gives up. A hook's other `Err(JobError::Io)` is
  not a failure: nothing commits, the job runs again, and no prefix is written.
  `charpente new`'s scaffold calls it in its echo property, where it passes
  trivially until a job declares `on_dead`; from then on it fails any run in which
  that hook failed. Its failure names the job and quotes what
  follows the prefix, the hook's error and then the job's (below).
- `events::<E: Event>(snap: &Snapshot) -> Result<Vec<E>, String>` and
  `events_scoped::<E: Event>(snap: &Snapshot, tenant: u64) -> Result<Vec<E>, String>
  where E::Scope: Tenant` — the durable event log read as your own event
  types, in log order: every row named `E::NAME` (for `events_scoped`, only
  those emitted in that tenant's scope, `tenant` being the raw id), decoded.
  `events_scoped` takes only a `#[event(scoped_by = ..)]` type; a global one
  does not compile there. They read every page of the log (`EVENTS_PAGE`
  rows a call), so a long run is read whole. A row is decoded only under the
  shape it was written with: a different fingerprint, a payload that does not
  decode, or bytes left over after it is an `Err` naming the event, the row
  id and the fix (read it with the type that wrote it), never a skipped row.
  Use them instead of scanning `EventRow` and decoding by hand.

`keys_are_per_effect` fails with one of:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
keys_are_per_effect: jobs <a> and <b> carry the same idempotency key <key> but not the same request (their <name|payload> differs) — a key carries exactly one request; only a re-issue from on_dead copies a key, and it copies the request with it
keys_are_per_effect: jobs <a> and <b> carry the same idempotency key <key> and neither is Dead — a key is copied only by a re-issue of a Dead job, so two live jobs under one key would send the effect twice
```

`outbound_settles_by_horizon` fails with:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
outbound_settles_by_horizon: job <id> ("<name>") is still Pending at <at> after the tail, at attempt <a>, due <due> — an outbound job that is due settles or retries to Dead; one that does neither was lost by the kernel
```

`<at>` and `<due>` are RFC 3339 times. A due time of `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`
is a job enqueued to run at once.

<!-- pinned -->

```text
dead_hooks_succeeded: job <id> ("<name>") is Dead and its on_dead hook failed: <hook error> — the job's own last error: <job error> — the Dead mark committed alone, so what the hook was to do (tell someone, re-issue the effect) did not happen; fix the hook and replay this seed
```

A worked `acked_implies_durable` example — a toy that writes one byte per
round and only claims the ack once its `sync` returns `Ok`:

```rust
use charpente::core::io::Disk;
use charpente_sim::Sim;
use charpente_sim::checks::{acked_implies_durable, is_fault_fallout};

/// Returns a fresh `drive` closure: each call performs one round, writing
/// the next byte and syncing before claiming its ack — never before.
fn drive() -> impl FnMut(&mut Sim) -> Result<Vec<String>, String> {
    let mut round: u64 = 0;
    move |sim: &mut Sim| {
        let file = match sim.disk().open("bytes") {
            Ok(f) => f,
            Err(e) if is_fault_fallout(&e.to_string()) => return Ok(vec![]),
            Err(e) => return Err(e.to_string()),
        };
        if let Err(e) = file.write_at(round, &[0xAA]) {
            let msg = e.to_string();
            return if is_fault_fallout(&msg) { Ok(vec![]) } else { Err(msg) };
        }
        if let Err(e) = file.sync() {
            let msg = e.to_string();
            return if is_fault_fallout(&msg) { Ok(vec![]) } else { Err(msg) };
        }
        let id = format!("byte-{round}");
        round += 1;
        Ok(vec![id])
    }
}

fn verify(sim: &mut Sim, acked: &[String]) -> Result<(), String> {
    let file = sim.disk().open("bytes").map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
    let len = file.len().map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
    for id in acked {
        let offset: u64 = id
            .strip_prefix("byte-")
            .expect("ack ids are \"byte-N\"")
            .parse()
            .expect("ack ids carry a numeric offset");
        if offset >= len {
            return Err(format!("{id} missing after restart (file len {len})"));
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

    // `sim`, not `sim.seed()`: the checker restarts the world you hand it, so
    // the `restart` coverage lands where the harness reads it and your
    // run's fault config is the one the property runs under.
    acked_implies_durable(sim, 5, drive(), verify)
}
```

248	### The outside world: remote models
249	
250	Outbound HTTP goes through the `Outbound` IO trait, to hosts the app
251	declares. In a sim, each declared host is a model you register: a `Remote`
252	that lives inside the run, runs on its seed, and answers each request
253	when the request reaches it. The wire between the kernel and the model
254	belongs to the sim, and the outbound fault axes act on that wire.
255	
256	Register one model per declared host, then build the outbound handle:
257	
258	- `sim.remote(host, model)` makes `model` the outside world behind `host`.
259	  One model per host: registering a host twice is a contract panic,
260	  `contract: sim.remote("<host>", …) registered twice`.
261	- `sim.outbound(hosts)` builds one process's handle, a
262	  `charpente_sim::outbound::SimOutbound`. `hosts` is the app's declared host
263	  list, passed as plain data. A host with no model is refused by name before
264	  anything runs:
265	
266	<!-- pinned -->
267	```text
268	sim: a mounted job calls <host>, which has no model — add sim.remote("<host>", …) before sim.outbound(…)
269	```
270	
271	The same text is a panic when a handle starts a call to a host that has no
272	model, such as one the list given to `sim.outbound` left out.
273	
274	A model implements `charpente_sim::outbound::Remote`, whose one method is
275	`fn handle(&mut self, call: &OutboundCall, rng: &mut Rng) -> OutboundReply`,
276	with `OutboundCall` and `OutboundReply` from `charpente::core::io` and `Rng`
277	from `charpente_sim::rng`. `call` is the request as the kernel built it:
278	`host: &'static str`, `method: HttpMethod`, `path: String` (path and query),
279	`headers: Vec<(String, String)>`, `body: Vec<u8>` and `key: IdempotencyKey`.
280	`OutboundReply` has no constructor: build it as a struct literal of its three
281	`pub` fields, `status: u16`, `headers: Vec<(String, String)>` and `body:
282	Vec<u8>` (the example below). `handle` runs when the request reaches the
283	remote, at its drawn delivery time, not when the kernel starts the call.
284	`rng` is the model's own seeded stream, keyed by the host's name, so a
285	model's variance (a payment that is sometimes declined, an LLM that sometimes
286	answers ambiguously) replays with the seed and moves no other draw. It offers `next_u64()`, `fill(&mut [u8])`,
287	`chance(p)` (true with probability `p`, which must lie in [0, 1]), `below(n)`
288	(uniform in `0..n`) and `between(lo, hi)` (uniform in `lo..=hi`). A model is
289	`Send + 'static`. It runs under the sim's world lock, so it must never call
290	back into the `Sim`.
291	
292	There are three ways to get a model. Each is a named choice, and none is a
293	default:
294	
295	- `charpente_sim::outbound::from_fn(f)` wraps a closure,
296	  `FnMut(&OutboundCall) -> OutboundReply`. The closure gets no `rng`, so
297	  write a `Remote` impl when the model needs variance.
298	- `Recorder::new()` answers 200 with an empty body and keeps every call it
299	  was handed, in delivery order. `calls()` reads them. It models
300	  fire-and-forget email.
301	- `Idempotent::header(name, model)` wraps an inner model in Stripe's
302	  idempotency semantics, keyed by the value of the header `name` (matched
303	  case-insensitively). `Idempotent::by(extract, model)` takes the key from
304	  any part of the request, through `extract: fn(&OutboundCall) ->
305	  Option<String>`. A repeated key with the same method, path and body gets
306	  the first reply again, and the inner model does not run. A repeated key
307	  with a different method, path or body gets a 409. A request with no key is
308	  applied every time, as Stripe does. `applied()` counts applications per
309	  key. A repeated key replays, so every count is 1, and the map says which
310	  keys reached the inner model: a retry that sent a fresh key shows up as a
311	  second entry, never as a 2. `inner()` reads the wrapped model. The key is
312	  what the app put in the request, never `OutboundCall::key`: a real remote
313	  never sees that field.
314	
315	A workload reads model state with `sim.with_remote::<M, _>(host, |m| …)`. The
316	closure borrows the model as its concrete type `M`, since a reference cannot
317	outlive the world lock. The closure runs under that lock, as a model does, so
318	it must not call the `Sim` either: return what you need and act on it after.
319	Naming a host with no model, or the wrong type, is a contract panic, and the
320	wrong-type text names both the type asked for and the one registered. A
321	wrapped model is read as its wrapper: `|m: &Idempotent<StripeModel>|`, then
322	`m.inner()`.
323	
324	The closure gets `&M`, never `&mut M`, so nothing reaches a model through
325	`with_remote`. A model the workload must change mid-run, such as one
326	calmed for the fault-free tail, shares state with it from registration: the
327	workload keeps a clone of an `Arc<AtomicBool>` and flips it between kernel
328	runs. The model reads it when a request reaches it, so a request already on
329	the wire meets the new state. This model does that, and draws its variance
330	from `rng`:

333	use charpente::core::io::{OutboundCall, OutboundReply};
334	use charpente_sim::Sim;
335	use charpente_sim::outbound::Remote;
336	use charpente_sim::rng::Rng;
337	use std::sync::Arc;
338	use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};
339	
340	/// An LLM that labels a message, and answers "unsure" one call in ten until
341	/// the workload calms it.
342	struct Classifier {
343	    calm: Arc<AtomicBool>,
344	}
345	
346	impl Remote for Classifier {
347	    fn handle(&mut self, call: &OutboundCall, rng: &mut Rng) -> OutboundReply {
348	        let label = if !self.calm.load(Ordering::Relaxed) && rng.chance(0.1) {
349	            "unsure"
350	        } else if call.body.windows(6).any(|w| w == b"urgent") {
351	            "urgent"
352	        } else {
353	            "routine"
354	        };
355	        OutboundReply {
356	            status: 200,

360	    }
361	}

363	/// Registers the model and hands back its switch. Before the fault-free tail

365	fn register(sim: &Sim) -> Arc<AtomicBool> {
366	    let calm = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false));
367	    sim.remote("llm.example", Classifier { calm: Arc::clone(&calm) });

372	`sim.outbound_deliveries()` returns every request that has reached a
373	remote, as `charpente_sim::outbound::Delivered { host: String, key:
374	IdempotencyKey, at: u64, handle: u64 }`.
375	`key` is the job's `OutboundCall::key`, which attributes a delivered call to
376	its job. `at` is the virtual arrival time in nanoseconds, and `handle` says
377	which `SimOutbound`, and so which process, sent it. Like `with_remote`, it
378	first runs every delivery due by now, so what it shows is current with the
379	clock.
380	
381	A request in flight at a crash still arrives; only its reply is lost. Models
382	belong to the run, not to the box, so `sim.restart()` leaves them and
383	every request already on the wire alone. The restarted process builds a new
384	handle with `sim.outbound(…)`. A reply goes only to the handle that started
385	its call, so a pre-restart reply has nowhere to land, even when the new
386	process reuses the old token. A cancelled call (`Outbound::cancel`) behaves
387	the same way: its request still reaches the remote at its delivery time, and
388	its completion is never handed back.
389	
390	Every call rolls each fault axis once, from that axis's own keyed stream,
391	whatever the other axes decide, and draws both of its latencies the same
392	way. So turning one axis on or off moves no other axis's draw. It can still
393	change what happens downstream: a call it refuses never reaches the model,
394	so the model's own `rng` sees one call fewer. Delivery and reply times are
395	drawn when the call starts. The call's fate is chosen from its rolls in a
396	fixed precedence: refused, else lost, else throttled, else delivered. A
397	delivered call may also be slow, and may lose its reply. Coverage counts
398	only what applies, so a refused call that also rolled a lost reply counts as
399	refused:
400	
401	| Axis (`FaultConfig` field) | The remote sees | The kernel sees | Coverage key |
402	|---|---|---|---|
403	| `outbound_refused` | nothing | an immediate transport error, `ConnectionRefused` | `fault:outbound_refused` |
404	| `outbound_lost_request` | nothing | silence, then its deadline | `fault:outbound_lost_request` |
405	| `outbound_lost_reply` | the call, applied | silence, then its deadline: the ambiguous case | `fault:outbound_lost_reply` |
406	| `outbound_throttle` | nothing (overloaded) | a 429 or 503 | `fault:outbound_throttle` |
407	| `outbound_latency` `(min, max)` and `outbound_slow` | the call, late | a reply late, or past the deadline (the LLM tail) | `fault:outbound_slow`; latency has none |
408	| `outbound_outage` `(start, length)` | nothing | every call to one host refused for the window, `ConnectionRefused`, through the tail's quiesce | `fault:outbound_outage` |
409	
410	`outbound_outage` is a window of virtual time, not a roll: it reads the
411	sim's clock, draws nothing per call, and `quiesce_outbound_faults` does not
412	end it, so an outage outlives the tail's quiesce and runs to its drawn end,
413	and `Drive::recover`'s tail runs on until the jobs it refuses settle or go
414	Dead. That is how a job reaches Dead in a sim, and `mark_dead_coverage` marks
415	`dead:<job>` for each one it reaches. The host is the one the universe's
416	first outbound call picks, from the hosts the app declares (the list given to
417	`sim.outbound`) in name order. The window is refused as `outbound_refused` is, and takes its place
418	in the precedence. A length of zero is off, and an app with no hosts makes
419	no call, so the axis is inert there.
420	
421	`outbound_latency` is a one-way range, drawn once for the request and once
422	for the reply, and a throttle answers after twice the request's draw.
423	`outbound_slow` adds think time between the request's arrival and the
424	reply's departure, uniform in [10·max, 100·max], or in [1 s, 100 s] when max
425	is zero. Every
426	completion handed back to the kernel also marks `outbound:completed`.
427	Duplicates are not an axis. In HTTP a duplicate is a retry after a lost
428	reply, and the sim produces those. Whether a duplicate applies twice is the
429	model's semantics, which is what `Idempotent` is for.
430	
431	`FaultConfig::default()`, which `Sim::new` uses, turns the five outbound
432	faults off and sets latency to 1–50 ms. `FaultConfig::none()` makes every
433	call instantaneous. A swarm run samples all six fields in
434	`sample_extended_fields`, each from its own stream, so the existing axes'
435	sampled values are unchanged:
436	
437	| Field | Swarm sample |
438	|---|---|
439	| `outbound_refused` | on with chance 0.25, at a rate from 0 to 0.049 in steps of 0.001 |
440	| `outbound_lost_request` | on with chance 0.25, at 0 to 0.029 |
441	| `outbound_lost_reply` | on with chance 0.25, at 0 to 0.029 |
442	| `outbound_throttle` | on with chance 0.25, at 0 to 0.099 |
443	| `outbound_slow` | on with chance 0.25, at 0 to 0.049 |
444	| `outbound_latency` | `(0, max)`, with max one of 0, 10 ms, 200 ms or 2 s, each with chance 0.25 |
445	
446	`outbound_outage` is not in a swarm sample. `charpente test --sim` draws it
447	from its own stream (`outbound_outage`) after the clock axes, and a
448	`run_universes_swarm!` suite never turns it on:
449	
450	| Field | App-harness sample |
451	|---|---|
452	| `outbound_outage` | on with chance 0.25; the start uniform in the first 2 s of virtual time; the length one of 60 s, 300 s, 1800 s or 4 h. The default policy (5 attempts, a 30 s doubling backoff, a 30 s timeout) survives the first two and is exhausted by the last two |
453	
454	### Calling the outside world in a sim
455	
456	An app with an outbound job is driven the way "Driving the whole app in a sim"
457	drives any app, with one addition: a model behind each declared host,
458	registered with `sim.remote` before `Drive::faulted_phase`. `Drive` builds each
459	kernel with `Kernel::with_outbound` over the sim's handle exactly when the app
460	declares hosts, and quiesces the outbound faults in the tail. Below the
461	helper, build the handle before the kernel, since
462	`sim.outbound(&app.outbound_hosts())` borrows the app that
463	`Kernel::with_outbound` takes. The workload below takes two orders under the
464	run's faults, then runs the fault-free tail ("A fault-free tail" above) and
465	calls the three outbound checkers:
466	
467	```rust
468	use charpente::core::job::JobRow;
469	use charpente::core::table::Id;
470	use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig, Method, Request};
471	use charpente::kernel::JobError;
472	use charpente::outbound::{Call, Host, IdempotencyKey, Reply};
473	use charpente::wire::WireU64;
474	use charpente::{Schema, Tx, View, Wire, job, jobs, route, routes, table};
475	use charpente_sim::Sim;
476	use charpente_sim::checks::{
477	    calls_have_durable_jobs, durable_corruption_fired, keys_are_per_effect,
478	    outbound_settles_by_horizon,
479	};
480	use charpente_sim::drive::Drive;
481	use charpente_sim::outbound::{Idempotent, Recorder};
482	use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
483	use std::time::Duration;
484	
485	#[table(global)]
486	struct Receipt {
487	    id: Id<Receipt>,
488	    sent: bool,
489	}
490	
491	#[job(
492	    global,
493	    retain_dead,
494	    outbound = "mail.example",
495	    retry(max = 3, backoff = "1s"),
496	    timeout = "5s"
497	)]
498	struct SendReceipt {
499	    order: u64,
500	}
501	
502	impl SendReceipt {
503	    fn call(&self, _tx: &Tx, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError> {
504	        Ok(Some(
505	            Call::post("/send")
506	                .header("idempotency-key", key.as_str())
507	                .form(&[("order", self.order.to_string())]),
508	        ))
509	    }
510	
511	    fn settle(self, tx: &mut Tx, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError> {
512	        match reply.status() {
513	            200 => {
514	                tx.put(&Receipt {
515	                    id: Id::from_raw(self.order),
516	                    sent: true,
517	                });
518	                Ok(())
519	            }
520	            s => Err(JobError::app(format!("mail.example answered {s}"))),
521	        }
522	    }
523	}
524	
525	#[derive(Wire, Serialize, Deserialize)]
526	struct OrderBody {
527	    order: WireU64,
528	}
529	
530	#[route(POST "/order", public)]
531	fn order(tx: &mut Tx, body: OrderBody) -> Result<WireU64, ApiError> {
532	    let id: Id<Receipt> = Id::from_raw(body.order.0);
533	    // The tail re-sends an order the phase left unanswered: one that landed
534	    // anyway is answered as placed, with no second receipt. The request is
535	    // the order's id alone, so a repeat is always the same request.
536	    if tx.get(id)?.is_some() {
537	        return Ok(body.order);
538	    }
539	    tx.put(&Receipt { id, sent: false });
540	    tx.enqueue(SendReceipt {
541	        order: body.order.0,
542	    });
543	    Ok(body.order)
544	}
545	
546	fn build_app(sim: &Sim) -> std::io::Result<App> {
547	    Ok(App::open(
548	        Box::new(sim.disk()),
549	        Schema::new().table::<Receipt>(),
550	        Box::new(sim.entropy()),
551	        AppConfig::default(),
552	    )?
553	    .mount(routes![order])
554	    .mount_jobs(jobs![SendReceipt])
555	    .outbound(Host::new("mail.example")))
556	}
557	
558	fn receipts_settle_under_faults(sim: &mut Sim) -> Result<(), String> {
559	    sim.remote(
560	        "mail.example",
561	        Idempotent::header("idempotency-key", Recorder::new()),
562	    );
563	    let requests: Vec<(Duration, Request)> = (0..2u64)
564	        .map(|order| {
565	            (
566	                Duration::from_secs(order),
567	                Request::new(Method::Post, "/order").json(&OrderBody {
568	                    order: WireU64(order),
569	                }),
570	            )
571	        })
572	        .collect();
573	    let drive = Drive::new(sim, build_app);
574	    let phase = drive.faulted_phase(&requests, Duration::from_secs(30))?;
575	    // The tail's power cycle may find a call in flight; the job is still
576	    // Pending, and its next call carries the same key. 600 s is past every
577	    // backoff and deadline, with room to spare; `recover` would run on past
578	    // it for a receipt still due there.
579	    let Some(recovered) = drive.recover(&phase, Duration::from_secs(600))? else {
580	        return Ok(());
581	    };
582	
583	    let snap = recovered
584	        .kernel
585	        .app()
586	        .db()
587	        .snapshot()
588	        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
589	    keys_are_per_effect(&snap)?;
590	    outbound_settles_by_horizon(&snap, recovered.wall)?;
591	    if let Err(e) = calls_have_durable_jobs(sim, &snap) {
592	        if durable_corruption_fired(sim) {
593	            sim.give_up("media corruption cut an enqueue whose call was made", e);
594	            return Ok(());
595	        }
596	        return Err(e);
597	    }
598	    let jobs = snap.scan::<JobRow>().map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
599	    if jobs.iter().any(|j| j.outbound_key.is_some()) {
600	        sim.cover("outbound:checked"); // no order committed, nothing checked
601	    }
602	    Ok(())
603	}
604	```
605	
606	Register it as `receipts_settle_under_faults require ["outbound:checked"]`. A
607	run in which no order committed passes all three checkers having checked
608	nothing, which is why the coverage key is marked only where an outbound job
609	exists. `Drive::recover` marks `dead:SendReceipt` for each receipt it took
610	to Dead, so `require ["outbound:checked", "dead:SendReceipt"]` also holds
611	that the receipt's Dead path ran under the batch's outages. The tail places
612	again what the phase left unanswered, so such a run
613	is rare. `Drive`'s faulted phase is one kernel: under a swarm's `sync_error`,
614	a kernel can poison early and `run` stops, leaving the rest of the phase's
615	script for the tail. A workload that wants more of its work done under
616	faults drops below the helper and runs the phase as a supervisor loop: restart
617	the process (`sim.restart_process()`, or `sim.restart()` once
618	`sim.disk_crashed()`), boot through `boot_through_fallout`, build a fresh
619	handle and kernel, and re-send in a new `SimSource` every request the last one
620	left unanswered, until the phase's time is up. Read that from the last
621	source's `answers()`, slot by slot, by the rule `Drive` applies: a `None`
622	slot, or a 5xx whose body is fault fallout
623	(`is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`). A 4xx, or a handler's own
624	5xx, is the app's answer and is not re-sent, so counting `responses()` to find
625	where the script stopped is not enough.
626	
627	**Why the key matters.** The platform mints the key and keeps it across every
628	retry, but only the app puts it in the request, and only the remote can act on
629	it. `tests/outbound.rs` in the `charpente` crate runs a workload like this one
630	as a swarm property: six payment jobs against
631	`Idempotent::header("idempotency-key", Recorder::new())`, three faulted rounds
632	with crashes, then the fault-free tail. Beside the three checkers it asserts
633	that the remote applied no charge twice, and that every recorded payment is one
634	the remote applied. Those two checks judge something only where a charge was
635	called again, so the property floors how many runs re-called a key, and how
636	many re-called it from a second process, rather than how many merely ran. Two
637	planted bugs show what the checks are for, each pinned to the seed that caught
638	it, and on both seeds the honest job passes with a verdict. `PayKeyless` leaves
639	the key header out of its call, so any re-call reaches the remote as a new
640	request. At seed `0xc064fe5aa31086a7` the first process's call to `/pay/2` was
641	applied, an injected fault ended the process before the reply settled, and the
642	next process called again: `double charge: pay.test applied /pay/2 2 times`. The
643	honest job goes through the same crash, and its second delivery is deduped. A
644	lost reply does the same thing inside one process: with every reply lost, the
645	keyless job's three attempts are three charges, where the keyed job's are one.
646	`PayTrusting` takes a 503 for a success, so a throttled call records a payment
647	the remote never made: seed `0xce5842050b68d0cb` fails with `phantom charge: job
648	2 recorded a payment, but pay.test never applied /pay/2`.
649	
650	### `charpente test --sim`
651

content.content:
### `charpente test --sim`

Run it from the app crate's own directory (or pass `--dir`):

```bash
charpente test --sim [--runs N] [--seed 0x…] [--master-seed 0x…] \
    [--filter S] [--jobs N] [--format human|json] [--inputs HEX] \
    [--faults-off AXIS,…] [--dir PATH]
```

- `--runs N` — how many runs, each on a fresh seed, **per selected check**
  (default 256; must be at least 1 — a green batch of zero runs proves
  nothing). `--universes` is gone; it is an unknown flag.
- `--seed 0x…` — bypass the batch entirely and run every selected test
  once, on this exact literal seed. Coverage `require`ments are skipped (one
  run can't be expected to hit everything a batch would). This is the
  replay flag: it is exactly what a failure's own `repro:` line uses. A
  replay is one run, so it shrinks nothing.
  It prints each check as `ok`, `FAILED` or `skipped`; under a skipped check,
  `skipped:` is the reason, `detail:` the run's own detail and `fired:` what
  fired in the run, and the `sim result:` line ends with the seed.
- `--inputs HEX` — with `--seed`, replay these input choices instead of the
  ones the seed draws: each `sim.input()` draw reads the next, and every draw
  past the end reads 0. A choice above its draw's range draws what it reduces
  to, and the run records it reduced. `HEX` is each choice as an unsigned
  LEB128 number, the bytes in lowercase hex, which is what a shrunk failure's
  `repro:` line prints. Anything else (an empty value, a character that is not
  lowercase hex, an odd length, a number cut off or past 64 bits) is a usage
  error naming the flag, so an unset `--inputs "$HEX"` never replays all zeros.
- `--faults-off AXIS,…` — with `--seed`, turn these `FaultConfig` axes off
  (any field but `corruption_scope`, which scopes two axes rather than being
  one). The axes are `write_error`, `sync_error`, `crash_apply`, `crash_torn`,
  `dir_entry_loss`, `bit_flip`, `misdirected_write`, `read_error`,
  `object_put_error`, `object_get_error`, `object_lost_ack`,
  `object_delete_error`, `conn_drop`, `net_spike`, `subscriber_stall`,
  `outbound_refused`, `outbound_lost_request`, `outbound_lost_reply`,
  `outbound_throttle`, `outbound_slow`, `outbound_latency`, `disk_latency`,
  `net_latency`, `clock_skew`, `clock_step_back`, `clock_downtime` and
  `outbound_outage`. The
  seed's config is sampled first and these are turned off after, so every
  other field is the seed's own. A name that is not an axis is a usage error
  that lists them.
- `--master-seed 0x…` — pick where the batch's seed chain starts, instead
  of fresh OS entropy, for a byte-identical repeat of an entire batch
  (every check's every run). Cannot be combined with `--seed`. The batch's
  last line is this flag with the batch's `--runs` and `--filter`. Without
  the flag, `CHARPENTE_SIM_MASTER_SEED=0x…` in the environment picks it
  instead ("Finding a one-sided property" below); the flag wins.
- `--filter S` — run only the check named `S` when there is one, and
  otherwise every check whose name contains `S`. A failure's `repro:` line
  names its check, so it replays that check alone even when another check's
  name contains it (`charge` and `charge_twice`). Filtering happens
  **before** any seed is drawn, so a filtered batch consumes a different (but
  still fully reproducible) prefix of the seed chain than an unfiltered one
  — this is why every individual failure's repro line carries its own
  run's seed rather than relying on the batch's master seed.
- `--jobs N` — how many runs to run in parallel (default: the host's
  available parallelism). Every run's seed is pre-derived on the main
  thread, in registry order, before any work is handed out, so `--jobs 1`
  and `--jobs 8` run the identical seed sequence and produce byte-identical
  reports — worker scheduling is unobservable.
- `--format human|json` — human is the default; `json` emits one object with
  every fact the human report prints, keys in this order: `master_seed`,
  `runs`, `passed`, `failed` and `skipped` (run totals over every check),
  `coverage`, `missing_coverage` (`{check, key}` pairs), `checks`,
  `failures`, `result` and `exit`. `result` is the human result line's word
  (`ok`, `FAILED` or `nothing tested`) and `exit` the code the run exits with,
  so a record read later still says whether the batch failed, an untested
  check included. A quick pass (`CHARPENTE_SIM_FIRST_RUNS`, "Finding a
  one-sided property" below) ends on one more key, `quick_pass`, as
  `{first_runs, full_runs}`, since its `result` and `exit` judged failed runs
  only; its `runs` is the runs it ran of each check. Under `--seed`, `seed`
  stands where `master_seed` does, since the replayed seed fed back as
  `--master-seed` would run another batch. It is
  followed by `inputs`, the choices `--inputs` gave in that flag's encoding,
  when the replay was given them, and `faults_off`, the axes `--faults-off`
  turned off in field order, when it was given those. Each of `checks`, in
  registry order, is `{check, status, passed, failed, skipped, distinct_inputs,
  drew_inputs, skipped_reasons}`: `status` is `ok`, `FAILED` or `untested`
  (under `--seed` too, where the human line says `skipped`), and
  `skipped_reasons` lists every reason, uncapped, as `{reason,
  count, first_seed}` by count descending then reason, `first_seed` being the
  seed of the reason's first run in run order, plus `detail` under `--seed`,
  the one run's own text. Each of `failures` lists every failing run, in seed order, as
  `{check, seed, config, fired, message, inputs, faults_off, first_message,
  not_shrunk, replays, repro}`, with `config` carrying every fault axis. A
  check's first failure is the one a batch shrinks: its `inputs` are
  `{name, value}` pairs of the shrunk run, `message` is the shrunk run's,
  `first_message` appears only when the shrink slipped to another message,
  `replays` counts the candidates tried and `repro` replays the shrunk run.
  With shrinking off (under `charpente test --mutants`, "The timeout follows
  the scope too" below) it is its own run instead, with `not_shrunk` saying
  why and `replays` 0; no other failure carries `not_shrunk`. Every other
  failure is its own unshrunk run: its own drawn `inputs`, `faults_off` `[]`,
  `replays` 0, no `first_message`, and a `repro` that is its seed alone.
  Seeds are hex strings. The two report different totals: the human result
  line's passed and failed count checks, and the JSON's top-level `passed`,
  `failed` and `skipped` count runs, each the sum of that field over
  `checks[]`.
- `--dir PATH` — the app crate directory to build and run sim tests from
  (default: `.`). This flag is consumed by the CLI itself; every other flag
  passes straight through to the sim binary the CLI builds and execs.

Exit codes: **0** no run of any selected check failed, every `require`d
coverage key was hit, and every selected check was tested by at least one run
(skipped runs are reported, not failed — see "Giving up" above; a green batch
says how many runs tested each check); **1** at least one run failed, a
coverage requirement went unmet, or a check tested nothing because every one of
its runs was skipped (its result line then says `FAILED`, or `nothing tested`
when no check was tested) — the batch itself completed, but something in it
was red or proved nothing. A `--seed` replay replays one run per check, not a
batch, so a skipped run there exits 0, and a quick pass judges failed runs
only, so it exits 1 for a failed run and for nothing else; **2** the batch
never got that far — a build failure, no
`tests/sim.rs` target found, an unrecognized flag, `--inputs` or
`--faults-off` without `--seed` or with a value they cannot read, a filter
matching no tests, or the sim binary failing to launch or exiting by signal. Exit code
2 means "rerun once this is fixed," not "here is a reproducible bug."

### Reading a batch

A batch prints, on stderr before any run starts, the line that names its master
seed, so a batch you kill still shows the seed that reruns it:

```text
running 4 sim checks, 256 runs each, under random injected faults (master seed 0x0000000000000001)
```

Its report, on stdout, has the shape of `cargo test`'s ("Giving up" above
shows two). Like `cargo test`'s, it closes with a line per check directly
above the result, so the last lines of the output carry every check's status
and counts beside the verdict. In order:

- **One failure block per failing check**: its first failure in seed order,
  shrunk ("Reading a failure" and "Shrinking a failure" below). The check's
  other failing runs print no block; its line counts them, and `--format json`
  lists each one.
- **A line per unmet requirement**: `sim coverage requirement failed in
  <check>: "<key>" never occurred in <n> runs`, with what to do about it. The
  `<n>` is every run of the check, and every one of them counts, failed and
  skipped runs included, so the key truly never fired.
- **The skipped runs' reasons**, under each check that skipped any, most
  frequent first and then in byte order, each with its count and the seed of
  its first run in run order, the same for any `--jobs`: `(first: --seed
  0x…)`. With `--filter <check>`, that seed replays a run that skipped for that
  reason and prints its detail. A check that
  tested nothing is headed `— never tested: every run was skipped`. A check
  lists at most eight reasons and counts the rest on one line; `\n`, `\r` and
  `\t` in a reason print as those two-character escapes, so every reason stays
  on one line. When a check tested nothing, one line follows the reasons,
  `a check that tested nothing proves nothing, so the batch fails: …`, which
  names the fixes ("Giving up" above shows it).
- **The checks that draw no inputs**, named, when any check with a tested run
  drew none: each of their runs tested the same scripted case.
- **A line per check**, in registry order: `check <name> ... <status>
  (<counts>)`. A run that passed or failed *tested* the check; a run that gave
  up was *skipped*. The status is `FAILED` when a run failed or a `require`d
  key never occurred, `untested` when no run tested the check, and `ok`
  otherwise. The counts are how many runs tested it (`52 tested`), how many
  distinct inputs those runs drew when it draws any (`203 tested over 181
  distinct inputs`, "Drawing inputs" above), how many failed when any did
  (`64 tested: 16 failed`), how many were skipped when any were (`52 tested,
  12 skipped`), and the keys that never occurred (`required "restart" never
  occurred`).
- **The result**: `sim result: ok` when every check line reads `ok`, `FAILED`
  when one reads `FAILED` or when one reads `untested` and another `ok`, and
  `nothing tested` when every one reads `untested`. A batch that reads `FAILED`
  or `nothing tested` exits 1. A quick pass ("Finding a one-sided property"
  below) judges failed runs only, so there an `untested` line beside an `ok`
  one reads `ok`, and only `FAILED` exits 1. The word is followed by how many
  checks passed, failed and (if any) were untested, and then how many runs
  tested each check, in the order of the check lines above it, an untested
  check as 0:
  `Runs tested per check, in the order above: 209, 251, 214 of 256.`, or
  `Runs tested: 251 of 256.` when the batch ran one check. There is no total
  across checks, because a total lets a check tested in 3 of its runs hide
  behind two tested in 250 of theirs.
- **The rerun command**: `rerun exactly this batch: charpente test --sim
  --master-seed 0x…`, with `--runs` when the batch ran another count than 256
  and `--filter` when it had one. Pasted, it prints this report again, byte
  for byte, for any `--jobs`. A batch run under `CHARPENTE_SIM_NO_SHRINK`
  ("Finding a one-sided property" below) did not shrink, and its line starts
  `CHARPENTE_SIM_NO_SHRINK=1 charpente test --sim`, so the pasted command
  does not shrink either. A quick pass's line carries
  `CHARPENTE_SIM_FIRST_RUNS=N` the same way, and its quick-pass line follows
  it.

There is no line for the faults that fired. To confirm that a fault a property
depends on actually happened, `require` its coverage key (`sim_tests! {
orders_charge_once require ["fault:outbound_refused"] }`): an unmet requirement
fails the check, and its line names the key. That makes "the refused reply was
exercised" a claim the batch checks rather than a number someone has to read.

The human report is for reading, not parsing: read `--format json` in a
program.

### Reading a failure, replaying its seed

A human-format failure looks like this (a pinned test in `charpente-sim`'s
harness holds its shape, these lines in this order):

```text
sim failure in receipts_exactly_once: exactly-once violated: hits 2, done 1 for key 3
  seed:   0x8bee1752811ae873
  fired:  fault:dir-entry: 3, restart: 7
  inputs: key=3, order=[1, 0]
  shrunk: 3 draws to 2, faults off: bit_flip, read_error, in 87 replays
  before shrinking: exactly-once violated: hits 3, done 1 for key 812
  repro:  charpente test --sim --filter receipts_exactly_once --seed 0x8bee1752811ae873 --inputs 03c801 --faults-off bit_flip,read_error
```

This is a check's first failure in the batch, shrunk ("Shrinking a failure"
below): every line but `before shrinking:` describes the smallest run the harness found
that still fails the check, and `repro:` replays exactly that run. Each line,
in order:

- The first line is that run's own `Err` message (or an absorbed panic
  payload) — the actual claim that failed.
- `seed` is the one `u64` that determined this entire run: virtual
  time, every entropy draw, the fault matrix's decisions and, unless the
  repro passes `--inputs`, every `sim.input()` draw.
- `fired` is what ACTUALLY happened: the run's coverage map, every
  fault and event that really occurred, with counts. This is the line to
  reason from. A high probability whose key is absent here never fired, and
  an explanation resting on it is wrong. `fired: nothing` is a real and
  valuable answer — it means no injected fault was involved and the failure
  is a plain bug. (This line exists because it once did not: a durability
  finding was attributed to `dir_entry_loss: 0.477` by three separate
  readers, none of whom could have known whether that axis fired, because
  the failure path discarded coverage entirely — docs/LEDGER.md 2026-09-07.)
- `inputs` is every `sim.input()` draw the run made, by name, in draw order
  ("Drawing inputs" above). A run that drew nothing has no `inputs:` line.
- `shrunk` says how far shrinking got: how many inputs the first failure
  drew and how many the shrunk run drew, counted as the `inputs:` line lists
  them; the fault axes it turned off (`none` when it needed them all); and
  how many runs it replayed. The shrunk run can draw more than the first: a
  fault turned off can let a loop run longer. `shrunk: nothing smaller fails, in N replays`
  means no smaller run failed the check, so the block is the first failure's
  own and its repro is the seed alone.
- `before shrinking` is the first failure's message, printed only when the shrunk run
  failed the check with another one (a slipped shrink, below).
- `repro` is not advice, it **is** the reproduction: paste that exact line
  and the same run happens again, byte for byte. `--seed` replays a literal
  seed; `--inputs` appears only when the shrunk run's choices are not the
  ones the seed draws, and `--faults-off` only when it turned axes off (both
  above). There is no separate "figure out how to reproduce this" step —
  the failure message already did that work. Replaying it prints the same
  block without `shrunk:` and `before shrinking:`, since a replay is one run and shrinks
  nothing.

The check's other failures in the batch print no block: its check line counts
them (`64 tested: 16 failed`), and `--format json` lists each one, unshrunk,
with a repro that is its seed alone.

The same discipline extends outward: `run_universes!`/`run_universes_swarm!`
(the frozen internal-suite macros the platform's own tests use) and
`charpente test --sim` share one seed→behavior mapping, except that only
`charpente test --sim` samples the clock axes. So `CHARPENTE_SEED=0x… cargo
test -p <pkg> --test <file>` and `charpente test --sim --seed 0x…` are the
same idea at two different layers, each replaying its own layer's run: a
failure's seed is always enough, on its own, to see the exact same run
again.

### Shrinking a failure

A failing run usually carries more than its bug: inputs that play no part, and
fault axes that were on but did nothing to it. So the harness replays the first
failure of each check with smaller choices and fewer faults, and keeps each
smaller run that still fails the same check. The last one it keeps is the run
the block shows. The rule is the same for every check.

It shrinks the recorded choice sequence, not the values (Hypothesis's approach):
each choice is the one its draw used, so a smaller choice is a smaller, simpler
value (`lo`, the first item, the identity order), and a draw past the end of
the choices reads 0. Its passes run in rounds, repeated until a whole round
keeps nothing:

1. delete chunks of the choices, 8, 4, 2 and then 1 long, from the end toward
   the start, and then whole items, last first. An item is the choices from
   one draw to the next draw of the same name, when that is two or more
   choices: an item drawn as a template, an acquirer and a target comes out
   in one step, where a cut that is not a whole item shifts every later draw
   and the run usually passes. So give the draws that make up an item the
   same names each time, as a loop does, and end the loop on a drawn "more"
   rather than a drawn count ("Drawing inputs" above);
2. set each choice to 0;
3. search each choice down toward 0 (galloping up from 1, then bisecting), so a
   small value that fails is found even when the values between it and the
   recorded choice pass;
4. turn off each fault axis that is on, one at a time, in `FaultConfig` field
   order. An axis is on when it could fire: a clock axis whose chance is 0 is
   off whatever its size, so `faults off:` never lists it;
5. lower equal choices together: for each nonzero value two or more choices
   hold, set all of them to 0 and then search them down toward 0 as one value,
   so a failure that needs the same entity drawn twice (the same lab, the same
   product) reaches the lowest one, where lowering either draw alone makes the
   two differ and passes. Then, only in a round where everything before kept
   nothing, an axis turned off counting as a keep, each pair of those choices
   the same way, for a value that also sits where the failure does not need
   it. A whole group costs one candidate and a search, as cheap as passes 2
   and 3, so whole groups are tried in every round, right after pass 4. The
   pairs wait because k equal choices make k(k-1)/2 of them, enough to spend
   the whole budget: run while the other passes can still shrink the run,
   they could leave on fault axes the failure does not need, or inputs larger
   than it needs. Waiting costs a whole round of the other passes first, so
   among many choices the budget can run out before a needed pair is tried;
   the shrunk run then still fails the check and replays, with more draws
   than it needs.

A round that keeps nothing ends the shrink on a local minimum: no step of these
passes shrinks the run and still fails. They do not search every smaller run,
so a smaller one that fails the check can still exist. A shrink that spends its
budget (below) ends where the budget ran out, which can be short of a local
minimum.

A candidate is kept when the same check fails, with any message. One that
passes or gives up is not kept, so a clock axis whose removal turns the failure
into a clock-excused skip stays on. A smaller input can move where faults land,
and a fault turned off can change how many inputs a run draws (a retry loop that
no longer retries). Neither breaks anything, because the harness judges a
candidate only by replaying it, exactly as the printed repro does.

Shrinking runs on the first failure of each check in seed order, never in
completion order, and each shrink depends only on its check, seed and first
failure. Its budget is 500 replays, counted rather than timed, so the block is
identical for any `--jobs` and on any machine. A shrink that spends the budget
stops with the smallest run found so far. Those replays run one after another,
so a check's shrink can take several times as long as the batch that found it;
under `charpente test --mutants` the harness does not shrink at all ("The
timeout follows the scope too", below). A workload that panics prints the
panic's message on stderr each time a shrink replay panics; the report itself is
on stdout, written once every shrink has finished.

**A slipped shrink.** Any failure of the same check counts, so the shrunk run
can fail it for another reason than the first did. The headline is then the
shrunk run's own message, `before shrinking:` keeps the original, and `repro:` replays the
shrunk run. The original is the seed alone: drop `--inputs` and `--faults-off`
from the repro. When the two messages name different bugs, fix the one the
repro shows, then rerun the batch.

### Re-basing a pinned property: `CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED`

Some properties fix their base seed (`run_universes_swarm_with!(BASE, N, …)`)
so their `floor:` rates have a stable denominator. That is right for a rate and
wrong for a correctness claim: a fixed base means the property only ever
examines the same N runs, while a green run reads as though it examined
the space.

`CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED=0x… cargo test -p <pkg> --test <file>` re-bases every
pinned property in that binary, so the claim "this property holds" can actually
be tested rather than assumed:

```text
charpente-sim [realtime]: re-basing 0x000000002eb20001 -> 0x00000000a11ce001 under
  CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED — coverage requirements, floors and ceilings skipped (they
  are rates measured at the pinned base)
```

Like `CHARPENTE_SEED`, it takes hex with or without `0x`, and `_` separators
are ignored, so a base copied from the source as written (`0x2EB2_5A10`) works
as is; a value that is not hex panics naming the variable it was read from.

Floors, ceilings and `require:` keys are skipped under the override, for the
reason the floor's own panic text gives: they are rates measured AT a base, so
evaluating them somewhere else compares against a denominator that was never
taken there.
What the mode tests is the property's own assertions, which are untouched.

**A correctness oracle should pass at every base.** If it passes at its pinned
base and fails at others, it is not flaky — it is failing, and the pinned base
is hiding it. Two realtime properties were found exactly that way
(docs/LEDGER.md 2026-09-07).

One caveat worth knowing before you chase a floor panic: an IO call consumes RNG
draws, so changing *where* an IO operation happens inside code a property never
names reshuffles every run at a pinned base. Floors move for that reason far
more often than they move because an oracle decayed.

So a floor that falls after such a change is re-measured, not defended and not
quietly lowered. Run the property before and after the change at the same ten or
more fresh bases (`CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED`) and compare the key's mean. It has
decayed if the after-mean sits more than one Welch standard error below the
before-mean, where that error is `sqrt(sd_before²/n_before + sd_after²/n_after)`
over the per-base counts. Within one standard error, the floor is re-set to its
new exact count at its pinned base, with both distributions recorded; beyond
it, the fall is the finding. A base where either binary fails on an unrelated,
named bug is left out of both sides, and the record says which. One standard
error is deliberately strict: pure noise crosses it roughly a sixth to a quarter
of the time, which errs toward stopping to look.

A cap that rises after such a change asks a different question, because a
give-up is not a lost verdict when the same run used to pass having
checked nothing. So judge the rise by the verdicts the property reached, over
the same ten or more fresh bases: count its passes that covered its reach key
(the key its `floor:` counts), and beside them its vacuous passes (runs
that passed without covering that key). A cap may rise only if the passes
covering the reach key did not fall by more than one Welch standard error.
Then the new give-ups replaced vacuous passes, not verdicts, and the cap is
re-set by its own convention, with both distributions recorded. If those
passes fell by more than one standard error, the rise is the finding. Neither
the reach key's own count nor the vacuous passes can decide it alone: 20 more
give-ups beside 1 fewer vacuous pass means 19 passes that checked something
became give-ups. A pinned cap can read the same
number on both binaries while the rate behind it moved, so the test runs
whenever the change could have moved it, not only when the pinned count did.
That is also why every capped property floors its reach key: without one, the
next change that costs it reach passes with every cap still met.

At a pinned base both bounds are exact counts. At an ambient base, where the
counts move batch to batch, both are margins over ten or more fresh batches.

An ambient give-up cap is the larger of two numbers:
- twice the largest fresh-batch count;
- the smallest k with P(Poisson(lambda) > k) < 1e-4, where
  lambda = n x U(x) / N. Here n is the runs in one batch, N the runs
  over all the fresh batches, and x the give-ups among them. U(x) is the exact
  one-sided 95% Poisson upper bound for x: 2.996 for x = 0, 4.744 for 1, and
  6.296 for 2.

The second number matters where give-ups are rare. When no batch gave up,
twice the largest count is 0, which one legitimately exhausted run fails.
When one batch gave up once, it is 2, which a healthy batch fails about once
in eighty. Where counts are large the first number is the larger, and the
second only confirms it.

Two worked examples for the WAL fault matrix, whose 10 fresh batches of
n = 512 make N = 5,120:
- **x = 0**, as measured. lambda = 512 x 2.996 / 5,120 = 0.30. P(> 3) is
  2.6e-4 and P(> 4) is 1.6e-5, so k = 4, and the cap is max(0, 4) = 4.
- **x = 1**, as ten bases including 0x9E7C000A would have read: one batch gave
  up once. lambda = 512 x 4.744 / 5,120 = 0.47. P(> 4) is 1.4e-4 and P(> 5) is
  1.1e-5, so k = 5, and the cap is max(2, 5) = 5, not 2.

An ambient reach floor is the mean less four standard deviations. That flakes
about once in thirty thousand batches if the counts are near normal, and fails
any batch that falls further. So an ambient floor catches a collapse, not a
drift. Kernel exactly-once's `job:done` spreads by about 4% of its mean (sd
19.1 on 485.2), so its floor sits about 16% below the mean. A fall half that size trips about one batch in
forty, which a change can pass by luck. The before-and-after comparison above
is the instrument that sees a move that small, so it runs whenever a change
could move an ambient floor's rate, as it does for a cap, and not only when a
batch goes red.

The directory barrier used to be the worst offender, because `sync_dir` is the
call a *durability* fix is most likely to add — one such fix moved floors in
three separate files in a single day. It now draws from its own fault stream, so
adding or relocating a barrier perturbs nothing else. A file sync with nothing
to flush is the other exception: it cannot fail and draws no fault, so syncing a
file that is already durable moves no roll. That is the shape most durability
fixes take after a power cycle. It still counts as a disk operation, so it
ticks an armed crash countdown and advances virtual time. No other IO call has
either treatment, so the caveat above still holds for the rest of them.

### Finding a one-sided property: `charpente test --mutants`

A green suite tells you your properties passed. It does not tell you they would
have **failed** if the code stopped working. A property that asserts something
true whether or not your job ran is *one-sided*: it costs time, reports success,
and is not evidence about anything.

This is not hypothetical. A helpdesk app built on charpente shipped five such
properties — deleting its entire SLA sweep loop left the suite green.
